title: Mock 1
introHtml:
Purpose: Modern CAT baseline. Format: 24 questions: 20 MCQ and 4 TITA. Time limit: 40 minutes. Marking: +3 for a correct answer, −1 for a wrong MCQ, 0 for a wrong TITA.

How the difficulty labels were assigned: they are expert judgement, scored on five things:

  • how dense and abstract the passage is
  • how many reasoning steps the question needs
  • how complex the question wording is
  • how close the distractors are to the correct option
  • how much time the question costs

They have not been checked against real candidates' responses. They describe the item, not your likely percentile.
diagnosticHtml:
If you missed… Work on
Q1, Q5 Telling the thesis apart from supporting points ("to begin with", "less X than Y")
Q4, Q7 Isolating the exact claim; the negation test for assumptions
Q13–Q16 Tracking whether a statement is the author's view or a cited one
Q15 Decoding double negatives before reading the options
Q10, Q16 Mapping features in analogy and application questions; checking both halves of a distinction
Q19, Q22 A paragraph's claim versus its topic; reading metaphors precisely
Q17, Q18 Locking chains of connectors and demonstratives

Pacing benchmark used in design: about 26–28 minutes for RC (about 2.5 minutes to read each passage, then about 1 minute per question) and about 12–14 minutes for VA. Under time pressure, take the fast marks first: Q3, Q9, Q11, Q20, Q24.

paragraphsHtml: For more than a century, the zebra's coat has served as a kind of Rorschach test for biologists, each generation reading into the stripes the preoccupations of its own science. Darwin confessed himself puzzled by them and tentatively suggested sexual selection. His successors were less modest. The stripes, it was variously argued, dazzled pursuing lions, broke up the animal's outline in the shimmering heat of the savannah, cooled the body by setting up small convection currents above black and white hair, or allowed individuals to recognise one another in the herd.

Most of these proposals share a weakness that is easy to overlook: they were advanced on the strength of their plausibility rather than tested against the animal's actual circumstances. The camouflage hypothesis, for instance, assumes that a lion sees what a human sees. Yet measurements of predator vision suggest that, beyond about fifty metres in daylight, a lion cannot resolve the stripes at all; the zebra simply appears as a grey, horse-shaped object. At the distances that matter for an ambush, the pattern is invisible. Nor do the temperature studies offer much comfort. When water-filled barrels were wrapped in striped and plain hides and left in the sun, the striped barrels were not reliably cooler.

The hypothesis that has fared best was, for a long time, the least glamorous. Biting flies—horseflies and tsetse flies in particular—carry diseases that are often lethal to equids, and zebras live in regions where such flies are abundant. Field experiments in which horses were dressed in striped coats found that flies approached them as often as they approached horses in plain coats, but failed to land: they overshot, bumped into the animal or veered away at the last moment. Video analysis suggests that the stripes interfere with the visual cues flies use to control their speed on approach, rather than making the animal harder to detect in the first place. Comparative data point in the same direction: across species and subspecies of zebra, the intensity of striping tracks the regional prevalence of biting flies more closely than it tracks predator density or temperature.

None of this licenses the conclusion that the puzzle is solved. The fly hypothesis explains why stripes might be advantageous; it does not explain why they are distributed as they are across the body, why the legs of some populations are more boldly marked than their flanks, or why other animals in fly-infested regions have not converged on the same solution. A trait that originated for one reason may also be maintained for others, and it would be surprising if a feature so conspicuous carried no social meaning at all for animals that live in large, shifting herds.

What the episode illustrates is less the triumph of one theory than a change in method. The older explanations were not foolish; they were untested. Progress came not from a more ingenious story but from the patient work of asking what a striped body actually does to a lion's eye, a fly's flight path or a barrel's temperature—and from a willingness to accept answers less elegant than the questions.
passages.notesTitle: Zebra stripes (biology; accessible)
passages.notesHtml:
How the passage is built:

  1. A history of the explanations offered for the stripes.
  2. Those explanations were plausible but untested, and testing undercuts camouflage and cooling.
  3. The fly hypothesis is the best supported, by field experiments, video analysis and comparative data.
  4. Even the fly hypothesis has limits.
  5. The moral: what changed was the method, not the winner.

paragraphsHtml: It is a commonplace of popular history that the railway abolished local time. Before the locomotive, so the story goes, every town kept its own noon, set by the sun over its church tower; after it, a single national hour was imposed from the capital, and the rhythms of provincial life were made to answer to a timetable. The story is not false, but it has the direction of causation slightly wrong, and in its eagerness to dramatise the triumph of the machine it misses what was most interesting about the change.

To begin with, local time was never as local as the legend implies. Long before the railways, the clocks that mattered to commerce—those of the post office, the exchange, the coaching inn—were frequently set not by the sun overhead but by the time of a larger town on which local business depended. A market town forty miles from a port might keep the port's time on market days and its own on Sundays. What existed was not a mosaic of sealed temporal islands but a loose hierarchy of reference points, negotiated according to who needed to coordinate with whom.

The railway companies did not sweep this arrangement away so much as add another layer to it. Their timetables ran on the time of the line's headquarters, and for decades many stations displayed two clocks, or a single clock with two minute hands, one for the trains and one for the town. Passengers grumbled, but they also adapted with considerable ingenuity, much as modern travellers manage time zones. In many countries the legal adoption of a uniform standard came a generation or more after the railways had made it convenient, and often only after courts had been forced to decide awkward questions—whether a lease expiring at midnight expired at the town's midnight or the railway's, whether a voter arriving at a polling station at a disputed hour had arrived too late.

Seen this way, standard time was less an imposition than a ratification. The state did not invent a national hour; it chose, among several hours already in use, the one that the most powerful networks had made indispensable, and gave it the force of law. That is a subtler kind of power than the legend allows, and in some respects a more durable one. A rule that merely codifies existing practice meets little organised resistance, because those who might object to it have already, in their daily arrangements, half-accepted it.

None of this is to deny that something changed. Solar noon had a kind of public legibility: anyone could check it against the sky. Railway time could be checked only against another clock, and ultimately against an authority one could not see. The shift was not from freedom to tyranny but from a time that was, in principle, available to every observer to a time that was available only through institutions. Whether that counts as a loss depends on how much one values the ability to verify for oneself the conventions by which one's life is ordered.
passages.notesTitle: Railway time (social history; moderate)
passages.notesHtml:
How the passage is built:

  1. The legend: railways imposed a single time.
  2. Correction 1: local time was already a hierarchy of reference points.
  3. Correction 2: railways added a layer. There were dual clocks for decades, and the law came late.
  4. The thesis: standard time was ratification, not imposition, and ratification is a subtler, more durable kind of power.
  5. Coda: something changed. Time became checkable only through institutions. Whether that is a loss is left to the reader.

paragraphsHtml: The earliest surviving recipe collections make frustrating reading for anyone who hopes to cook from them. Quantities are rarely given; times are expressed, if at all, as the length of a prayer or of a walk to the well and back; instructions end with the injunction to cook the dish until it is done. It is tempting to see in this vagueness the mark of a culinary culture that had not yet learned to measure. The more plausible reading is the opposite. These texts were not written for people who did not know how to cook. They were aide-mémoires for people who did—reminders of a combination, a sequence or a proportion that the practised cook would then adjust by eye, by smell and by the feel of dough under the palm.

The precise modern recipe, with its level teaspoons and oven temperatures, answers to a different situation: a readership that cannot be assumed to share any prior competence. Its rise tracks the growth of populations who had left the households in which cooking was learned by watching, and of publishers who needed a text that would work for a stranger in an unknown kitchen. Precision, in other words, was a technology for transmitting skill across a break in the chain of apprenticeship.

Like most such technologies, it was enormously successful and quietly costly. A recipe that specifies everything can be followed by anyone, but it also implies that following is all there is to cooking. The cook who has learned from such texts may produce a reliable cake while remaining unable to say why it rose, or what to do when the flour is different, the oven runs hot or the eggs are small. The knowledge that the old aide-mémoire took for granted—how a batter should look when it is ready—has not been transmitted; it has been designed out, replaced by instructions that make it unnecessary under standard conditions and leave the cook stranded under any others.

It would be easy to turn this into a lament for lost authenticity, but that would be a mistake of a different kind. The tacit knowledge of the traditional kitchen was also a means of exclusion: it could be acquired only by those admitted to the household, and it reproduced, along with its techniques, the hierarchies of that household. The precise written recipe democratised competence even as it thinned it. What it could not do was replace the slow education of the senses on which genuine adaptability depends.

The interesting question, then, is not whether precise recipes are better or worse than the older kind, but what each presupposes about its reader. Every instruction encodes a guess about what the person following it already knows. The more confident the guess, the shorter the text; the less confident, the longer and more explicit it must become—until, at the limit, the instructions attempt to substitute entirely for the experience they were once meant only to supplement.
passages.notesTitle: Recipes and tacit knowledge (cultural history; moderate)
passages.notesHtml:
How the passage is built:

  1. Vague early recipes were reminders for experts.
  2. Precise recipes transmitted skill once apprenticeship broke down.
  3. The cost: knowledge was "designed out", leaving cooks stranded.
  4. The counterweight: tacit knowledge excluded people, while precise recipes democratised competence but thinned it.
  5. The real question is what each kind of text presupposes about its reader.

paragraphsHtml: We are inclined to believe that people should be judged only for what lies within their control. The driver who glances at the radio for a moment and runs over a child seems, on reflection, no more culpable than the driver who glances away for the same moment on an empty road; the difference between them is a matter of whether a child happened to be crossing. If blame tracks what an agent chose, and both chose the same thing, the blame should be the same. Yet almost nobody feels this way about the two drivers—including, very often, the drivers themselves.

One response is to treat the feeling as an error: an understandable but irrational tendency to let outcomes contaminate our judgement of conduct. On this view the reflective verdict is correct, and the task of moral philosophy is to bring our reactions into line with it. The difficulty is that the principle behind the verdict, applied consistently, proves ruinously expansive. Our choices are shaped by a temperament we did not select, by an upbringing we did not arrange and by circumstances that tested some of us and spared others. The citizen of a peaceful country who would, in another place and decade, have joined a persecuting mob has done nothing wrong; but neither has he done anything right. If luck must be subtracted from every assessment, it is not obvious that anything remains to be assessed.

A second response accepts the reaction and abandons the principle: outcomes simply do bear on what we are answerable for, and the unlucky driver really is worse placed morally than the lucky one. This is more faithful to experience, but it courts a different absurdity. It implies that a person's moral record can be improved or ruined by events that occur after she has done everything she will ever do—that a prudent decision can turn reckless in retrospect because the world declined to cooperate.

Perhaps the dilemma is sharp only because it assumes that "judgement" names a single thing. There is a difference between the verdict of blame, which ought to attend to what the agent did and could have known, and the burden of responsibility, which may properly fall more heavily on the one whose act ends in disaster. The unlucky driver is not more wicked than the lucky one, but it would be strange, and a little chilling, if he felt no differently. His remorse is not a confusion about his culpability; it is the recognition that his life has become entangled with a harm in a way that the other driver's has not. We would think less of him, not more, if he consoled himself with the reflection that, strictly speaking, he was no worse than anyone else who has ever glanced at a radio.

To say this is not to dissolve the problem but to relocate it. The question shifts from whether luck can affect what we deserve to how many distinct things we are doing when we hold one another to account.
passages.notesTitle: Moral luck (moral philosophy; abstract, difficult)
passages.notesHtml:
How the passage is built:

  1. The puzzle: the control principle against our reaction to the two drivers.
  2. Response 1 (cited view): treat the reaction as an error. Applied consistently, this principle is "ruinously expansive".
  3. Response 2 (cited view): let outcomes matter. This "courts a different absurdity": moral records changing after the fact.
  4. The author's view: separate the verdict of blame (conduct and knowledge) from the burden of responsibility (which can be heavier after a disaster). Remorse is fitting, not a confusion.
  5. The problem is "relocated", not dissolved.

Track ownership. Most wrong options here describe Response 1 or Response 2 accurately.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best captures the main point of the passage?

options.html: The fly hypothesis has emerged as the best-supported account of zebra stripes, showing that comparative evidence can settle what plausibility cannot.
Because a lion cannot resolve stripes at hunting distances, explanations based on concealment from predators have had to be abandoned.
Testing what stripes actually do, rather than what they might plausibly do, has narrowed the field without closing the question.
The early explanations of zebra stripes reveal more about the preoccupations of biologists than about the function of the stripes.

questions.explanationHtml:
Passage evidence:

  • "None of this licenses the conclusion that the puzzle is solved." (P4)
  • "What the episode illustrates is less the triumph of one theory than a change in method." (P5)

Why C: C captures both halves of the conclusion. Testing replaced plausibility, and that "narrowed the field": camouflage and cooling are undercut, and flies are best supported. But it did not "close the question".

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Overstatement and wrong focus. "Best-supported" is accurate, which is why A tempts. But "comparative evidence can settle what plausibility cannot" is wrong twice. The author says the puzzle is not settled, and the decisive shift was testing in general (vision measurements, barrels, field experiments), not comparative evidence in particular.
  • (B) Part for whole. The lion-vision finding is one result from P2. The passage is about method and the overall state of the evidence.
  • (D) Misreads the opening hook. The Rorschach image is a framing device. The author's actual verdict is that the old explanations "were not foolish; they were untested". D turns a rhetorical opening into the thesis.
questions.takeawayHtml: an option can be right about a detail ("best-supported") and still wrong as a main idea. Check every clause against the conclusion.

questions.stemHtml: The author notes that flies approached horses in striped coats "as often as" horses in plain coats primarily in order to:

options.html: suggest that stripes give little protection against flies, since flies were no less inclined to approach striped horses than plain ones.
locate the effect of the stripes in the moment of approach and landing, not in whether the animal is detected.
indicate that flies, like lions, cannot make out the pattern until they are close enough for it to matter.
show that the field experiments needed the support of comparative data before any conclusion could be drawn.

questions.explanationHeading: Q2. Answer: B — purpose of a detail (moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Passage evidence:

  • Flies "approached them as often… but failed to land".
  • The stripes "interfere with the visual cues flies use to control their speed on approach, rather than making the animal harder to detect".

Why B: Flies found the striped horses just as often, so the stripes do not stop detection. The effect must lie in the approach and landing. B states this.

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Reversal. Equal approach rates might seem to show the stripes give no protection. But the flies "failed to land", and protection lies in landing, not approaching.
  • (C) Misattribution. The point about resolving stripes only at close range belongs to lions (P2). Nothing says flies cannot make out the pattern. The passage implies the stripes act on flies' vision.
  • (D) Unsupported. The comparative data "point in the same direction". They corroborate the experiments; they do not rescue an inconclusive result.
questions.takeawayHtml: for "primarily in order to" questions, read the sentence after the detail. It usually states the detail's job.

questions.stemHtml: All of the following are presented in the passage as limitations of the fly hypothesis EXCEPT:

options.html: It does not account for the way in which striping is distributed across different parts of the body.
It does not explain why other animals living among biting flies have not evolved similar patterns.
It leaves open the possibility that the stripes are maintained partly for other reasons, such as social signalling.
It does not explain why flies approach horses in striped and plain coats with roughly equal frequency.

questions.explanationHtml:
Passage evidence: P4 says the hypothesis "does not explain why they are distributed as they are across the body… or why other animals… have not converged", and adds that stripes "may also be maintained for others [reasons]… social meaning".

Why D: The equal-approach finding is not something the fly hypothesis fails to explain. The hypothesis explains it: flies approach but cannot land.

Why the others are listed limitations:

  • (A) P4: distribution across the body.
  • (B) P4: why other animals have not converged.
  • (C) P4: maintenance for other reasons, such as social meaning.

Distractor mechanism: true but irrelevant, recast as a weakness.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously undermine the comparative evidence that the author cites in the third paragraph?

options.html: Horses in striped coats were also bitten less often by mosquitoes, insects that locate their hosts mainly by smell rather than by sight.
Corrected survey data show striping following predator density as closely as it follows the prevalence of biting flies.
Lions hunt mostly at dusk and after dark, when their ability to resolve fine patterns is even poorer than in daylight.
Several antelope species living in the same fly-infested regions as zebras have plain coats without any striping at all.

questions.explanationHtml:
The claim under attack: striping "tracks the regional prevalence of biting flies more closely than it tracks predator density or temperature".

Why B: The evidence is a comparison: flies predict striping better than the alternatives. If corrected data show predator density predicting it just as well, the comparative edge disappears, and with it the support.

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Wrong target. Mosquito bites concern the field experiments and perhaps the visual mechanism, not the cross-population comparison. A is also the longest and most technical option, which can make it look important.
  • (C) Strengthens a different point. Poorer lion vision at dusk further damages the camouflage hypothesis. It does nothing to the comparison.
  • (D) Out of scope, and already conceded. The comparison is "across species and subspecies of zebra", so antelopes fall outside it. The author already lists other animals' lack of stripes as an open question in P4.
questions.takeawayHtml: if the claim is comparative ("more closely than"), the best weakener erases the comparison, not the subject in general.

questions.stemHtml: The author's principal disagreement with the "commonplace of popular history" is that it:

options.html: treats standard time as imposed on local practice, when it largely gave legal force to an hour that was already dominant.
overlooks how long towns resisted the railway companies' hours before the state finally intervened on their behalf.
assumes that towns kept time by the sun, when their commercial clocks were in fact set by the capital.
neglects the courts, whose rulings on leases and polling hours forced governments to invent a national hour.

questions.explanationHeading: Q5. Answer: A — author's principal disagreement (difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
Passage evidence:

  • The story "has the direction of causation slightly wrong".
  • "standard time was less an imposition than a ratification… the one that the most powerful networks had made indispensable".

Why A: The principal disagreement concerns what standard time was, a ratification rather than an imposition. A states this.

Why the others are wrong:

  • (B) Unsupported. The passage shows passengers adapting, not towns resisting, and the state never "intervened on their behalf".
  • (C) Partial truth plus distortion, the strongest trap. C echoes a real supporting point from P2: town clocks were not simply solar. But it misstates that point. The passage says clocks were set by "a larger town on which local business depended", in "a loose hierarchy of reference points", not "by the capital". And P2 opens with "To begin with", which marks it as a premise that prepares the P4 thesis, not as the principal disagreement.
  • (D) Distortion. The courts decided awkward questions, but the author explicitly denies that the state "invent[ed] a national hour".
questions.takeawayHtml: "principal" or "primary" disagreement means the thesis. Signposts like "to begin with" mark supporting points.

questions.stemHtml: The author refers to stations that displayed two clocks mainly in order to illustrate that:

options.html: passengers resisted railway time with enough success to force the companies to display the town's hour as well.
the railways' influence on timekeeping was felt chiefly within the stations, while the life of the town went on largely unaffected.
town clocks were abandoned only gradually, as stations made railway time increasingly visible to the public.
for a long period, railway time was layered on top of town time rather than substituted for it.

questions.explanationHeading: Q6. Answer: D — purpose of an example (easy)
questions.explanationHtml:
Passage evidence: "did not sweep this arrangement away so much as add another layer to it… for decades many stations displayed two clocks".

Why D: "Layered on top of rather than substituted for" paraphrases "add another layer… [not] sweep away".

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Unsupported cause. The second clock is never attributed to passenger resistance. Passengers "grumbled" and "adapted".
  • (B) Overreach. The railways made a standard "convenient" and one hour "indispensable", so their influence went well beyond the stations. The author corrects the mechanism of that influence, not its size.
  • (C) Wrong claim illustrated. The two-clock example shows coexistence. It says nothing about town clocks being "abandoned gradually", which the passage never describes.

questions.stemHtml: The author's claim that ratification is "in some respects a more durable" form of power than imposition depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.html: A rule that provokes little organised opposition is, for that reason, harder to dislodge.
The state is generally weaker than the commercial networks whose established practices it chooses to codify.
Rules imposed against existing practice are usually reversed once the authority behind them begins to weaken.
People who have half-accepted a convention in practice will come to endorse it fully once it acquires legal force.

questions.explanationHtml:
The argument:

  • Premise: a codifying rule "meets little organised resistance".
  • Conclusion: so ratification is "in some respects a more durable" form of power.

The gap: the premise is about resistance and the conclusion is about durability. The bridge is the assumption that a lack of organised opposition makes a rule harder to dislodge. That is A.

Negation test: suppose opposition had no bearing on how hard a rule is to dislodge. The premise would then no longer support "more durable", so A is required.

Why the others are wrong:

  • (B) Irrelevant comparison. The argument never ranks the strength of the state against the networks.
  • (C) Stronger than needed. The argument needs only that ratified rules are more durable "in some respects". It does not need imposed rules to be "usually reversed". Negate C and the argument survives.
  • (D) Beyond the argument. Half-acceptance is enough. Full endorsement is never required.
questions.takeawayHtml: an assumption is the minimum bridge between premise and conclusion. Options that say more than the argument needs (C, D) are classic traps.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best describes the author's stance in the final paragraph?

options.html: Wistful: the author regrets that people can no longer order their lives by the visible movement of the sun.
Untroubled: the author regards the change as a reasonable price for the coordination that standard time made possible.
Even-handed: the author identifies a real shift in who could check the time but declines to pass judgement on it.
Suspicious: the author implies that time kept by unseen institutions lends itself to abuse by those who control it.

questions.explanationHtml:
Passage evidence:

  • "None of this is to deny that something changed."
  • "The shift was not from freedom to tyranny."
  • "Whether that counts as a loss depends on how much one values…"

Why C: The author identifies a real shift: verification became possible only through institutions. Whether that is a loss is explicitly left to the reader's values.

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Too emotional. Nothing expresses regret, and "not from freedom to tyranny" rules out nostalgia for freedom.
  • (B) Too settled. The author does not call the change a "reasonable price". The cost–benefit verdict is left open.
  • (D) Overreach. "An authority one could not see" concerns who can verify the time. The passage never suggests abuse.
questions.takeawayHtml: when an author ends with "whether X depends on…", choose the stance that withholds the verdict.

questions.stemHtml: According to the passage, the absence of quantities in the earliest recipe collections is best explained by the fact that:

options.html: cooks of the period had no reliable instruments with which to measure weight, volume or cooking time.
their readers could supply by judgement what written quantities would otherwise have specified.
the households that kept them guarded their methods and left the texts incomplete on purpose.
traditional cooks prized variation in a dish above producing it the same way on every occasion.

questions.explanationHtml:
Passage evidence: "aide-mémoires for people who did [know how to cook]… that the practised cook would then adjust by eye, by smell…"

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) This is the "tempting" reading that the author rejects outright: "The more plausible reading is the opposite."
  • (C) Fusion. It welds P4's exclusion theme onto an invented motive, the deliberate omission of quantities.
  • (D) Plausible but unstated attitude. The passage never mentions valuing variation.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is most analogous to the precise modern recipe as the author characterises it?

options.html: A conductor's annotated score, which reminds experienced players of interpretive choices they have already made.
A family's unwritten method of curing meat, learned only by the children who work alongside their parents.
An old road map that once guided travellers well but now misleads them because the roads have changed.
A machine's instruction card, which lets a new hire run it correctly but says nothing about faults.

questions.explanationHtml:
What the analogy must match:

The precise recipe (passage) Option D
written for a stranger with no prior skill a new hire
works "under standard conditions" runs the machine correctly
leaves the user "stranded under any others" says nothing about faults

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) This is the analogy for the old aide-mémoire, a reminder for experts.
  • (B) This is the analogy for tacit, exclusive household knowledge.
  • (C) A different failure mode. C fails because it becomes obsolete. The precise recipe does not go out of date; it fails only outside standard conditions.
questions.takeawayHtml: list two or three structural features before reading the options. A and B are faithful analogies to the other items in the passage.

questions.stemHtml: The passage suggests each of the following about the tacit knowledge of the traditional kitchen EXCEPT that it:

options.html: could be acquired only by those admitted to the household in which it was practised.
survived, in explicit form, in the precise recipes that took the older texts' place.
carried with it the social hierarchies of the households through which it passed.
was what allowed a cook to adapt when ingredients or conditions departed from the usual.

questions.explanationHtml:
Passage evidence: the knowledge "has not been transmitted; it has been designed out".

Why B: B says the opposite of the passage.

Why the others are suggested by the passage:

  • (A) P4: "acquired only by those admitted to the household".
  • (C) P4: "reproduced… the hierarchies of that household".
  • (D) P4: "the slow education of the senses on which genuine adaptability depends". P3 makes the same point with the cook stranded by different flour or a hot oven.

questions.stemHtml: In the third paragraph, the statement that certain knowledge has been "designed out" most nearly means that this knowledge has been:

options.html: made unnecessary in ordinary conditions by the form of the instructions, and so never handed on.
set aside by publishers, who judged that most readers would rarely need it in a modern kitchen.
forgotten over time, because modern readers cook less often than members of earlier households did.
superseded by instructions that achieve more consistent results than intuitive judgement could.

questions.explanationHeading: Q12. Answer: A — phrase in context (moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Passage evidence: the gloss is in the same sentence. The knowledge was "designed out, replaced by instructions that make it unnecessary under standard conditions".

Why the others are wrong:

  • (B) Invented agent and motive. No publisher's judgement is described. "Designed out" describes how the text works, not anyone's decision.
  • (C) Wrong mechanism. The knowledge is not transmitted in the first place, because of the text's design. Nothing is said about how often people cook.
  • (D) Unsupported comparison. "More consistent results than intuitive judgement could" is never claimed. The author stresses that such cooks are stranded outside standard conditions. D tempts because precise recipes do produce "a reliable cake".
questions.takeawayHtml: in vocabulary-in-context questions, the meaning is usually in the clause right next to the phrase. Read it before your own sense of the word takes over.

questions.stemHtml: The author introduces the citizen of a peaceful country primarily in order to:

options.html: show that outcomes beyond an agent's control properly bear on what that agent deserves.
suggest that those raised in peaceful societies deserve credit for virtues that circumstance never tested.
illustrate that the control principle, consistently applied, leaves little that could still be judged.
argue that our reactions to other people are shaped by upbringing and so cannot be relied upon.

questions.explanationHeading: Q13. Answer: C — purpose of an example (moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Passage evidence: the example sits between "applied consistently, proves ruinously expansive" and "it is not obvious that anything remains to be assessed".

Why C: The citizen shows that the control principle, applied consistently, empties moral assessment.

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Misattribution. That outcomes bear on desert is Response 2's claim, not the point of this example.
  • (B) Reversal. "Neither has he done anything right." The citizen gets no credit.
  • (D) Distortion. The example says upbringing shapes our choices. It does not argue that our reactions are unreliable. Treating reactions as an error is Response 1's position, and this example is used against Response 1.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following most accurately represents the author's own position, as distinct from the views the author discusses?

options.html: The reflective verdict is correct; the unlucky driver's remorse, though natural, reflects a mistake about his culpability.
Outcomes bear on what we are answerable for, so the unlucky driver is genuinely the more blameworthy of the two.
Once "judgement" is seen to name more than one thing, the problem of moral luck simply disappears.
Blame should track conduct and knowledge, though responsibility can weigh unequally on agents who acted alike.

questions.explanationHeading: Q14. Answer: D — author vs cited views (difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
Passage evidence:

  • Blame "ought to attend to what the agent did and could have known".
  • Responsibility "may properly fall more heavily on the one whose act ends in disaster".

Why D: "agents who acted alike" captures the identical conduct of the two drivers.

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Response 1. It also contradicts the author's line "His remorse is not a confusion about his culpability."
  • (B) Response 2. The author says the unlucky driver "is not more wicked".
  • (C) Contradicts the final paragraph: "not to dissolve the problem but to relocate it."
questions.takeawayHtml: in "view 1, view 2, my view" passages, label each paragraph's owner as you read.

questions.stemHtml: None of the following can be inferred from the passage EXCEPT:

options.html: The author believes that the lucky driver deserves no blame, since his inattention happened to cause no harm.
The author regards bringing our reactions into line with reflective verdicts as the proper task of moral philosophy.
The author denies that the unlucky driver's remorse must rest on an error about his own culpability.
The author regards the second response as closer to the truth than the first, since it is more faithful to experience.

questions.explanationHtml:
Decode the question first: "None… can be inferred EXCEPT" means three options cannot be inferred and one can. Find the one supported option.

Why C: "His remorse is not a confusion about his culpability." Denying that his remorse must rest on an error is directly supported.

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Contradicted. For the author, blame tracks "what the agent did and could have known". The lucky driver did the same thing, so he is no less blameworthy. The reason A gives (no harm resulted) is outcome-based, which is exactly what the author's blame verdict excludes.
  • (B) Misattribution. This is Response 1 ("On this view…"), a position the author goes on to criticise.
  • (D) True premise, unsupported ranking. The author does call the second response "more faithful to experience". But the author then says it "courts a different absurdity" and sets both responses aside in P4. D turns one conceded advantage into an overall verdict.
questions.takeawayHtml: rewrite double-negative questions ("Which ONE can be inferred?") before reading the options. Also watch for options that quote a real concession and then overextend it, as D does.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following situations best illustrates the distinction drawn in the fourth paragraph?

options.html: Two surgeons make the same minor lapse; one patient dies, the other recovers. Both receive the same reprimand, yet the surgeon whose patient died feels bound to meet the family.
Two surgeons make the same minor lapse; one patient dies, the other recovers. Only the surgeon whose patient died is reprimanded, and she alone meets the family.
Two surgeons operate, one carefully and one carelessly, and both patients recover. Only the careless surgeon is reprimanded, and neither feels any need to contact the families.
Two surgeons make the same minor lapse; one patient dies, the other recovers. Both receive the same reprimand, and both regard the matter as closed once it is issued.

questions.explanationHtml:
The scenario must show two things together:

  1. The same blame for the same conduct.
  2. A different burden of responsibility for the one whose act ended in disaster.
Option Same conduct? Same blame? Heavier burden on the one whose act ended in disaster? Verdict
A Yes Yes Yes (feels bound to meet the family) Matches
B Yes No (outcome decides the censure) — Response 2
C No (careful vs careless) — No disaster Different contrast
D Yes Yes No (both treat it as closed) Missing half

Why D is the strongest trap: it gets the blame half exactly right. But the author says it would be "strange, and a little chilling" if the unlucky one "felt no differently", and that "we would think less of him" for consoling himself that way. D is the attitude the author criticises.
questions.takeawayHtml: when a distinction has two parts, check that the option shows both. Close distractors usually get one part right.

questions.stemHtml: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4) below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in this sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.html: The practice, however, was less passive than it sounds.
Readers in early modern Europe often kept commonplace books, notebooks into which they copied memorable passages under headings such as "Fortune" or "Ambition".
Over the years, then, such a notebook became a record not so much of what its owner had read as of how he had learned to read.
Deciding whether a line from a tragedy belonged under one heading or another was already a judgement about what the line meant.

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct order:

  1. 2 introduces commonplace books. Every other sentence depends on it ("The practice", "such a notebook", "one heading or another").
  2. 1 says the practice was "however, less passive than it sounds". This contrasts with the mechanical-sounding "copied" in 2.
  3. 4 gives the reason: choosing a heading was already a judgement.
  4. 3 concludes: "Over the years, then…"

Rejected orders:

  • 2413: 4 has already shown the practice involves judgement, so 1's "however… less passive" has nothing left to contrast with.
  • 2134: "then" in 3 draws the conclusion before its reason, and 4 is left dangling.
  • Any other opener: 1, 3 and 4 all need something earlier to refer back to.

questions.stemHtml: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4) below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in this sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.html: But once the deck began to move, many walkers adjusted their stride to keep their balance, falling into step with the sway and amplifying it.
Ordinarily, these sideways pushes, delivered out of step with one another, cancel out.
On its opening day, a new pedestrian bridge began to sway from side to side as crowds crossed it.
Its engineers had tested the structure against the vertical forces of walking, but not against the small sideways push that every footstep also delivers.

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct order:

  1. 3 describes the event: the bridge sways.
  2. 4: "Its engineers" refers back to the bridge in 3.
  3. 2: "these sideways pushes" refers back to 4's push. Ordinarily the pushes cancel out.
  4. 1: "But once the deck began to move…" contrasts with 2's "ordinarily".

Locked links:

  • 4 must come before 2, because "these" needs a referent.
  • 2 must come before 1, because "But" needs the "ordinarily" to contrast with.
  • 4 cannot open, because "Its" needs a noun before it.

So 3421 is the only valid order.

questions.stemHtml: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4, 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.html: Its rules are rarely written down, yet violations are noticed instantly and resented intensely.
A long line outside a restaurant persuades passers-by that the food must be good, and so tends to lengthen itself.
A queue is one of the few institutions that strangers assemble, without discussion, within seconds.
That is why someone who cuts in provokes more anger than a delay of the same length caused by a slow cashier.
What the queue enforces is not efficiency—a crowd served at random would often be served just as quickly—but a particular idea of fairness, in which priority is earned by arrival.

questions.explanationHtml:
The coherent paragraph is 3-1-5-4:

  • 3: strangers assemble queues spontaneously.
  • 1: the queue's unwritten rules are enforced intensely.
  • 5: what it enforces is fairness by arrival, not efficiency.
  • 4: "That is why" cutting in angers people more than an equal delay.

Why 2 is odd: Sentence 2 is about queues, but it treats a queue as a signal: a long line advertises quality and grows itself. The paragraph's subject is the queue as an unwritten norm of fairness. Nothing in 2 connects to "rules", "fairness" or "cutting in". It also cannot be slotted in:

  • 1's "Its rules" must follow 3. Placed between them, 2 would make "Its" refer to the restaurant.
  • 4's "That is why" needs 5 directly before it.
questions.takeawayHtml: ask what the paragraph claims, not just what it is about.

questions.stemHtml: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4, 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.html: The duration of the waggling run encodes distance, longer runs indicating more distant sources.
Nestmates who follow the dance then fly out and search the indicated area, using scent to pinpoint the flowers.
The scientist who first decoded the dance was met with scepticism from colleagues who doubted that insects could communicate symbolically.
A forager returning to the hive with news of food performs a figure-of-eight "waggle dance" on the vertical comb.
The angle of the waggling run relative to the vertical encodes the direction of the food relative to the sun.

questions.explanationHtml:
The coherent paragraph is 4-5-1-2. Swapping 5 and 1 also works and does not change the answer.

Why 3 is odd: the other four describe how the dance works, from performance to response. Sentence 3 is about how scientists received the discovery.

questions.stemHtml: The passage below is followed by four alternative summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
bodyHtml: Restorers once aimed to return a damaged painting to the appearance it had when it left the artist's studio, filling losses so seamlessly that no viewer could tell where the original ended. The modern profession is more cautious. Because every intervention is an interpretation, and interpretations date, restorers now favour treatments that can be reversed, and retouching that, while invisible at normal viewing distance, can be detected on close inspection. The goal is no longer to deceive the eye but to let the painting be read as a whole without pretending that its history of damage never happened. What has changed is less the restorer's skill than the restorer's idea of honesty.

options.html: Restorers now favour reversible treatments because the seamless retouching carried out by earlier generations has physically deteriorated.
Repairs have shifted from concealing damage to being reversible and detectable, a change of ethics more than of skill.
Restorers have given up retouching in favour of treatments that leave a painting's history of damage open to view.
Improved techniques let restorers make repairs that no viewer can detect and that can later be fully undone.

questions.explanationHtml:
What the summary must keep:

  • the shift from concealment to reversible, detectable repair
  • the change being one of honesty, not skill

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Misreads "interpretations date". That means interpretations go out of fashion. It does not mean the old retouching physically deteriorated, which is an invented cause.
  • (C) Close but wrong. The paragraph does say restorers no longer pretend the damage "never happened". But restorers have not "given up retouching". They still retouch, in a way that is invisible at normal viewing distance and detectable only up close. C turns detectable repair into no repair.
  • (D) Contradicted twice. "No viewer can detect" contradicts "can be detected on close inspection", and "improved techniques" contradicts "less the restorer's skill".

questions.stemHtml: The passage below is followed by four alternative summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
bodyHtml: When a language borrows a word, it rarely borrows the word's full range of meaning. A term that in its source language names a whole family of activities may arrive in the borrowing language attached to just one of them—the one that happened to matter at the moment of contact. Borrowing tends to fix a word to whatever situation first brought speakers of the two languages together, so that loanwords often preserve, like insects in amber, a narrow slice of a cultural encounter. A language's borrowings can therefore be read as a rough record of what its speakers needed words for, and from whom, at particular moments in their history.

options.html: Borrowed words lose their original senses gradually as speakers adapt them, so loanwords show how a culture's needs have changed.
A language's loanwords reveal which foreign cultures shaped it most deeply over the course of its history.
Loanwords keep the meaning they had in their source language, preserved like an insect in amber after contact ends.
Loanwords tend to carry only the sense that mattered when two languages met, so they map past needs and sources.

questions.explanationHtml:
Why D: It has the mechanism (only the sense that mattered at contact is borrowed) and the conclusion (loanwords map what speakers needed words for, and from whom, its "sources").

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Wrong timing. The narrowing happens at borrowing ("fix a word to whatever situation first brought speakers… together"). It is not gradual drift afterwards.
  • (B) Overgeneralises. "Which cultures shaped it most deeply" is a claim about overall influence. The paragraph claims only "a rough record of what… speakers needed words for, and from whom, at particular moments". B sounds measured, which makes it a strong trap.
  • (C) Misreads the metaphor. Amber preserves "a narrow slice", not the full original meaning. The paragraph's first sentence says a language "rarely borrows the word's full range of meaning", which contradicts C.
questions.takeawayHtml: pin down exactly what a metaphor preserves. Summary distractors often stretch it.

questions.stemHtml: There is a sentence missing from the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and decide where (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence fits best.
questions.insertSentenceHtml: On this view, city birds are not choosing a better channel for their message; they are shouting, and the shift in pitch is simply what shouting sounds like.
questions.placementParagraphHtml: Birds that live in cities often sing at a higher pitch than their rural relatives. ___(1)___ The obvious explanation is noise: traffic produces low-frequency sound, and a song pitched above it is more likely to be heard. ___(2)___ Some researchers have argued, however, that the higher pitch is not a targeted adjustment at all but a by-product of singing louder, since birds that raise their volume tend also to raise their pitch. ___(3)___ If so, the change may carry costs as well as benefits, because in several species females prefer lower-pitched songs, which they associate with larger and healthier males. ___(4)___

options.html: Option 1
Option 2
Option 3
Option 4

questions.explanationHtml:
What the sentence needs: "On this view… not choosing a better channel… they are shouting" requires the by-product-of-loudness view to come directly before it.

Gap Fits? Reason
1 No No view has been stated yet.
2 No It would follow the noise explanation, which says birds are choosing a better channel, so "this view" would contradict its own referent.
3 Yes It follows "a by-product of singing louder" and restates that view vividly. "If so…" then continues naturally.
4 No The paragraph has already moved on to the consequences, so going back to restate the view breaks the progression.

questions.stemHtml: There is a sentence missing from the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and decide where (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence fits best.
questions.insertSentenceHtml: Deception, in this account, was never the active ingredient; it merely accompanied the things that were.
questions.placementParagraphHtml: For decades it was assumed that a placebo works only if the patient is deceived into believing it is a real drug. ___(1)___ A number of trials have since tested this assumption by giving patients pills that were openly described to them as inert. ___(2)___ Surprisingly, many of these patients reported meaningful relief, in some studies comparable to that produced by conventional placebos. ___(3)___ One possibility is that what matters is not belief in the pill but the ritual surrounding it: the consultation, the prescription, the act of taking something at regular intervals. ___(4)___

options.html: Option 1
Option 2
Option 3
Option 4

questions.explanationHtml:
What the sentence needs: "Deception, in this account, was never the active ingredient; it merely accompanied the things that were." It requires an account of what does work.

Gap Fits? Reason
1–2 No No explanation has been offered yet.
3 No (the main rival) The surprising result has been reported, but "the things that were" has no referent until the ritual list appears.
4 Yes It follows the ritual list (consultation, prescription, routine). "The things that were" refers to that list.
