paragraphsHtml: Liberal accounts of civil disobedience usually list its conditions as if they were items on a checklist: the act must be illegal, conscientious, non-violent and public, and the person who commits it must be willing to accept the legal penalty. Of these, publicity tends to receive the least attention, as though it were merely a matter of not sneaking about. Yet it is publicity that does most of the theoretical work. A secret violation of the law, however principled, addresses no one; it is a private refusal. A public violation, by contrast, is a form of speech directed at the majority—an appeal to principles that the disobedient claims the majority already holds but has failed to apply. The other conditions follow from this. Non-violence matters because one does not persuade a fellow citizen by injuring him; willingness to accept punishment matters because it shows that the appeal is made from within the shared order rather than against it.

Critics have long objected that this last requirement is servile. Why, they ask, should a person who is right about an unjust law also submit to the penalty for breaking it? The objection has force against a moralising version of the theory, in which punishment is accepted as a kind of penance. It has less force against the version sketched here, in which accepting the penalty is not an admission of guilt but a credential: evidence, offered to sceptical onlookers, that the act is not simply self-interested law-breaking wearing the costume of principle.

What has changed is the economy in which such credentials circulate. When the means of making an act public were scarce—when it required a crowd, a newspaper willing to report, a courtroom to supply a stage—publicity was itself costly, and its cost did some of the work of distinguishing the conscientious from the opportunistic. Today almost any act can be made public at negligible expense, and the publicity of an act therefore tells observers very little about the seriousness of the person who performs it. The burden of signalling has shifted almost entirely onto the willingness to pay a price.

This shift has an awkward consequence. If the price is what persuades, there is a temptation to seek it out—to stage arrests and court penalties because they confer credibility—and the disobedient act risks becoming a performance of sacrifice whose audience is impressed by the suffering rather than moved by the argument. That would invert the original logic, in which the penalty mattered only as a guarantee that an argument was being made in good faith. The appeal to shared principles, the content of the address, would become secondary to the spectacle of its cost.

The remedy is not to abandon any of the traditional conditions but to remember their order of dependence. A sacrifice that carries no intelligible appeal to the majority's own commitments is not civil disobedience made more convincing; it is something else, however admirable, that has borrowed the name.
passages.notesTitle: Civil disobedience and publicity (political philosophy; difficult)
passages.notesHtml:
Map of the argument:

Paragraph Point
P1 Publicity does the theoretical work. Disobedience is an address to the majority, an appeal to principles the majority already holds. The other conditions follow from this.
P2 Critics call accepting punishment servile. The author replies that accepting the penalty is a credential, not a penance.
P3 Publicity is now cheap, so the job of signalling has moved to the willingness to pay a price.
P4 The risk: price-seeking turns disobedience into a spectacle of sacrifice.
P5 The remedy is to keep all the conditions but remember their order of dependence: the appeal comes first.

paragraphsHtml: Histories of insurance often begin with mathematics. In the standard telling, the calculus of probability, worked out by a handful of seventeenth-century thinkers, made it possible for the first time to put a price on uncertainty, and the insurance industry followed as a practical application of the new science. The story has the appeal of a clean lineage, but it runs into an awkward chronological fact. Marine insurance was a thriving business in the trading cities of Italy some three centuries before anyone had formalised the mathematics that was supposedly its precondition.

What made it possible was not a theory of chance but a change in the form of a contract. Earlier merchants had managed the hazards of sea trade chiefly through the sea loan, under which a lender advanced money for a voyage and forfeited repayment if the ship was lost. The arrangement bundled together two quite different things: credit, for the merchant who needed capital, and protection, for the merchant who feared loss. It also attracted the suspicion of authorities who saw in the high rates charged on such loans a disguised form of usury. The premium contract dissolved the bundle. A merchant who had capital of his own could now buy protection alone, paying a fixed sum in advance to an underwriter who promised compensation in the event of loss; no loan, and therefore no interest, was involved at all.

How were such premiums set without probability theory? Largely by judgement, and the judgement drew on information that no formula could have captured: the reputation of the captain, the condition of the vessel, the season, rumours of pirates or war, the price other underwriters had already accepted. Underwriters rarely bore a whole risk themselves; they took a share, and their willingness to do so was itself information to those deciding whether to take the next. An underwriter known to be careful could, simply by signing first, make a risk easier to place. Pricing was thus social before it was statistical. It depended on dense networks in which news travelled quickly and reputations could be lost in an afternoon.

Nor did mathematics, when it arrived, transform marine underwriting as thoroughly as the standard story implies. Probability theory is most powerful when risks are numerous and alike, so that individual uncertainties average out over a large pool. Human lives approximate that condition well enough for actuarial tables to be useful. Voyages do not. Each combined a particular ship, crew, cargo, route and season, and the number of voyages that were genuinely comparable was small. For a long time the best guide to a voyage's danger remained the informed opinion of people who knew the sea, the ships and the men who sailed them.

The point is not that mathematics was irrelevant to insurance, but that the institution was invented by people who had no need of it. What they needed—and built—was a way of separating risk from credit, and a market in which judgements about risk could be shared, tested and priced.
passages.notesTitle: The origins of marine insurance (economic history; moderate)
passages.notesHtml:
Map of the argument:

Paragraph Point
P1 The standard story is that mathematics came first. The chronology refutes it: insurance existed before the mathematics.
P2 The real innovation was a contract. The premium contract separated protection from credit, which the sea loan had bundled together.
P3 Premiums were priced by social judgement and shared information.
P4 Probability theory has limits with heterogeneous voyages.
P5 Mathematics was not irrelevant, but the institution did not need it at its invention.

paragraphsHtml: Disputes about punctuation are conducted with a fervour that would be surprising if the stakes were only typographical. A misplaced apostrophe on a shop sign can provoke letters to newspapers; arguments about the final comma in a list have divided editors for generations. The intensity suggests that people take punctuation rules to have the same kind of authority as rules of grammar, so that to break one is to make a mistake rather than a choice. The history of the marks themselves suggests otherwise.

For most of their existence, punctuation marks were not rules at all but aids to performance. Texts were read aloud, and the marks told a reader where to breathe, where to pause briefly and where at length. They were added, often inconsistently, by scribes, readers and later printers, and a single manuscript might carry the marks of several hands, each guiding a different reading. Readers who disagreed about the sense of a passage could, quite literally, mark it differently. Only gradually, as silent reading became the norm, did the marks come to be understood as indicators of grammatical structure—signals not of where the voice should rest but of how the clauses of a sentence relate to one another.

The two functions have never fully separated, and much of the heat in modern disputes comes from treating one as if it were the other. A comma placed where a speaker would pause may be condemned as grammatically unjustified; a comma demanded by grammatical analysis may be resisted because it chops up a sentence that reads smoothly without it. Each side appeals to a standard the other does not recognise, and each concludes that the other simply does not know the rules.

It would be more accurate to say that there are no rules of the kind either side imagines. Grammar, in the linguist's sense, describes regularities that speakers follow whether or not they have been taught them; an English speaker who has never opened a style guide does not put the article after the noun. Punctuation enjoys no such grounding. It is a technology of the page, learned rather than acquired, and its conventions are best understood as solutions to a practical problem: how to stop a reader from misconstruing a sentence. The useful question to ask of a comma is therefore not whether it is correct but whether it forestalls a likely misreading at a tolerable cost in fluency.

This is not a licence for anarchy. Conventions have a value that does not depend on the merits of any particular convention, much as the value of driving on one side of the road does not depend on the superiority of that side. A writer who punctuates by personal judgement alone, however sensible each choice, forces readers to learn a private system—and no reader can be expected to master a new one with every book. That cost may exceed whatever clarity the system gains. The case against treating punctuation as grammar is not a case for treating it as self-expression.
passages.notesTitle: The authority of punctuation (language; moderate)
passages.notesHtml:
Map of the argument:

Paragraph Point
P1 People treat punctuation rules as if they had the authority of grammar.
P2 Historically, punctuation marks were aids to reading aloud, and only later became grammatical signals.
P3 Modern disputes confuse these two functions.
P4 There are no rules of the grammatical kind. Punctuation is a learned technology for preventing misreading, so the test is misreading prevented against fluency lost.
P5 Conventions still have value as shared conventions. Idiosyncrasy costs the reader.

paragraphsHtml: For several decades, the case for culture in animals rested on a method of elimination. Researchers compiled the behaviours of different populations of a species—how they cracked nuts, groomed one another, used leaves to collect water—and identified those that were common in some places and absent in others. Where a difference could not be explained by the local environment or by genetic differences between populations, it was attributed to social learning: the animals did things differently because they had learned from different neighbours.

The method was always vulnerable. An absence of ecological explanation is not the same as an absence of ecological cause, and critics were quick to point out that a behaviour found in one forest but not another might reflect some feature of the habitat that researchers had simply failed to measure. Each new survey that failed to find an ecological difference strengthened the case only a little, since another unmeasured variable was always available. The inference to culture was, in effect, an inference from ignorance: whatever was left over once the known explanations had been subtracted.

More recent work has tried to observe transmission directly. In one kind of experiment, a few individuals in a wild population are trained to solve a feeding puzzle in one of two ways and then released back into their groups. If the trained solution spreads, and groups seeded with different solutions end up doing things differently, the role of social learning is no longer inferred from what is left over; it is watched as it happens. Such experiments have shown that some birds not only copy a technique but come to prefer the local variant even after discovering the alternative, which looks a good deal like conformity to a tradition.

It would be a mistake, however, to treat these results as settling the older argument. An experiment demonstrates that a population can sustain a tradition; it does not show that the differences observed between wild populations arose that way. The two methods answer different questions, and the evidence from one does not automatically transfer to the other. What the experiments do accomplish is to remove the objection, made in advance of any evidence, that animals could not maintain arbitrary local behaviours by social means. Once that possibility is established, the burden shifts: it becomes reasonable to ask critics what unmeasured ecological factor they have in mind.

Whether any of this amounts to culture depends on what is required of the word. If culture means behaviour transmitted socially and maintained as a local tradition, the case is now strong for a number of species, among them birds, whales and several primates. If it means a tradition that accumulates—each generation building on the modifications of the last, so that the result exceeds what any individual could invent alone—the evidence is far thinner. That is the more interesting question, and the honest answer is that we do not yet know how unusual our own species is.
passages.notesTitle: Culture in animals (animal behaviour; moderate–difficult)
passages.notesHtml:
Map of the argument:

Paragraph Point
P1 The method of elimination.
P2 The critics' objection: an unmeasured feature of the habitat could explain the difference (an "inference from ignorance"). New surveys help only a little.
P3 Seeding experiments let researchers watch transmission happen, including conformity.
P4 These experiments do not settle the question about variation in the wild, but they remove the objection in principle and shift the burden onto the critics.
P5 Culture as tradition: strong evidence. Culture as cumulative: thin evidence. The question of human uniqueness is open.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following, if false, could be seen as supporting the author's account of why the willingness to accept punishment matters?

options.html: Making an act of law-breaking public was once considerably more costly than it is now.
Accepting the legal penalty for an act of disobedience amounts to conceding that one acted wrongly.
Onlookers are often inclined to suspect that those who break the law are acting out of self-interest.
An appeal to shared principles cannot be made by means that injure the people to whom it is addressed.

questions.explanationHtml:
How to work this type: negate each option. The answer is the option whose negation supports the author's account. Here, the account under test is the one about why accepting punishment matters.

The author's account: accepting the penalty "is not an admission of guilt but a credential". It is evidence that the appeal is made in good faith from within the shared order.

Option by option:

  • (B) correct. Negated: "accepting the penalty does not amount to conceding that one acted wrongly." That is exactly the author's reply to the critics in P2.
  • (A) wrong. Negated: "publicity was never more costly than now." This contradicts P3. It weakens the author's story about how signalling shifted, so it does not support anything.
  • (C) wrong. Negated: "onlookers are not inclined to suspect self-interest." The credential is offered to sceptical onlookers. Without scepticism the credential has no job, so the negation undercuts the account.
  • (D) wrong. Negated: "an appeal can be made by injuring people." This undercuts the P1 rationale for non-violence. It is also about the wrong condition.
questions.takeawayHtml: write out the negation of every option before judging any of them. The trap is choosing the option that is true according to the passage. C and D are both true, but their negations weaken the account.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following practices would the author most likely recommend to a group planning an act of civil disobedience today?

options.html: Secure the widest possible media coverage, since it is publicity that turns a private refusal into an address to the majority.
Seek out the heaviest available penalty, since the willingness to pay a price is now what chiefly persuades observers.
Decline to accept any legal penalty, since submitting to punishment concedes the authority of an unjust law.
Make clear which commitments already held by most citizens the challenged law violates, and accept the penalty that follows.

questions.explanationHeading: Q2. Answer: D. Author would recommend (difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "The remedy is not to abandon any of the traditional conditions but to remember their order of dependence." A sacrifice without "an intelligible appeal to the majority's own commitments" is not civil disobedience.

D puts the appeal first and keeps the penalty as a supporting credential, which is the author's order.

Why the other options fail:

  • (A) It sounds like P1 ("publicity does most of the theoretical work"). But P3 says publicity is now cheap and "tells observers very little". Maximising coverage is not the remedy. This is a scope trap: true of the theory, wrong as advice for today.
  • (B) This is the temptation the author warns against in P4 ("seek it out… court penalties"). It reverses the author's advice. It is tempting because P3 really does say the burden "has shifted almost entirely onto the willingness to pay a price".
  • (C) This is the critics' view (servility), which the author rejects.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following sets of words best captures the central concerns of the passage?

options.html: Disobedience, media, sacrifice, spectacle
Disobedience, publicity, credential, appeal
Disobedience, punishment, servility, penance
Publicity, newspapers, cost, opportunism

questions.explanationHtml:
What runs through the whole passage:

  • Disobedience and publicity: P1, P3.
  • Credential: the penalty as credential (P2), the signalling problem (P3), and "confer credibility" (P4).
  • Appeal: P1 and the remedy in P5.

Why the other sets fail:

  • (A) "Sacrifice" and "spectacle" belong only to the P4 warning, and "media" is a P3 detail. This is the part-for-whole trap; CAT 2020's anarchism keyword question used the same mechanism. A also leaves out "appeal", which is both the foundation (P1) and the remedy (P5).
  • (C) "Servility" and "penance" come only from the critics' objection in P2.
  • (D) "Newspapers" and "opportunism" are details from P3. D also drops disobedience itself.
questions.takeawayHtml: for a keyword-set question, each word must recur across the passage. If a word belongs to a single paragraph, it doesn't belong in the set.

questions.stemHtml: The author's recommendation that we "remember their order of dependence" implies that:

options.html: accepting punishment matters only as a guarantee for an appeal, and not the reverse.
publicity should again be made costly, so that it can resume the signalling role it once performed.
the traditional conditions should be ranked according to how much each demands of the disobedient.
non-violence, rather than publicity, is the condition from which the others ultimately derive their importance.

questions.explanationHeading: Q4. Answer: A. Implication across paragraphs (difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
The pieces you need:

  • P1: the other conditions "follow from" publicity understood as an address.
  • P4: "the penalty mattered only as a guarantee that an argument was being made in good faith".
  • P5: "order of dependence".

Put together, the penalty depends on the appeal for its value, not the other way round. That is A.

Why the other options fail:

  • (B) A plausible remedy the author never proposes. The author keeps the conditions as they are and reorders our understanding of them.
  • (C) The wrong ordering principle. The order is about logical dependence, not about how much each condition demands of the person.
  • (D) Misattribution. P1 makes publicity, understood as address, the foundation. Non-violence is derived from it.

questions.stemHtml: The passage suggests each of the following about the sea loan EXCEPT that it:

options.html: tied a merchant's protection against loss to the act of borrowing money.
could be regarded by some authorities as a way of charging interest in disguise.
allowed a merchant to obtain protection against loss without taking on any debt.
shifted the loss of the borrowed sum onto the lender if the ship was lost.

questions.explanationHtml:
Why C is the exception: protection without debt describes the premium contract, not the sea loan. This is a misattribution, and it is the only option that misdescribes the sea loan.

The three options the passage supports:

  • (A) It "bundled together… credit… and protection".
  • (B) "Suspicion… a disguised form of usury".
  • (D) The lender "forfeited repayment if the ship was lost": the borrowed sum was lost to the lender.

questions.stemHtml: In the second paragraph, "the bundle" refers to:

options.html: the combination, within one contract, of financing for a voyage and cover against its loss.
the package of a loan and the high interest charged on it, which some authorities regarded as usurious.
the set of hazards—storms, piracy, war—that a merchant faced on any single voyage.
the shares of a single risk taken up by several underwriters acting together.

questions.explanationHeading: Q6. Answer: A. Phrase in context (moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "The arrangement bundled together two quite different things: credit… and protection." "The bundle" is therefore that pairing, held within one contract.

Why the other options fail:

  • (B) Close distractor. It pairs the loan with its interest. That is the usury concern, a separate point raised in the next sentence.
  • (C) Hazards are listed in P3 as inputs to pricing, not as what was bundled.
  • (D) Shared underwriting comes from P3. It is a different kind of "bundling" (syndication) that the passage never calls a bundle.
questions.takeawayHtml: resolve a pointer phrase like "the bundle" back to its antecedent sentence. Don't resolve it to the nearest topic.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following situations is most analogous to the limitation of probability theory described in the fourth paragraph?

options.html: A casino can predict its annual profits closely, even though the outcome of any single spin of the wheel is unpredictable.
A doctor relies on clinical intuition because the relevant studies have never been carried out in her region.
An insurer of rare, one-of-a-kind artworks finds statistical tables of little help and relies on specialists' appraisals.
A bank prices its millions of small loans by credit score because scoring is cheaper than interviewing each borrower.

questions.explanationHtml:
The limitation in P4: probability works when risks are "numerous and alike". Voyages were few and each was unique, so informed experts outperformed the tables.

Matching each option to that structure:

Option Cases few and unique? Experts outperform statistics? Verdict
(C) artworks Yes, one-of-a-kind Yes, specialists' appraisals Fits
(A) casino No, a large pool Statistics work Shows probability's strength
(D) bank loans No, a large pool Statistics work (and are cheap) Shows probability's strength
(B) doctor Not stated Intuition used Wrong reason

Why B is the strongest trap: the doctor uses intuition because studies "have never been carried out", a contingent gap that research could fill. The voyages resisted statistics by their nature: genuinely comparable cases were few.
questions.takeawayHtml: an analogy must match the reason for the outcome, not only the outcome.

questions.stemHtml: The author's primary purpose in the passage is to:

options.html: argue that marine insurance was priced socially rather than statistically, and stayed so long after probability arrived.
show that the mathematics of probability has been of little real value to the business of insurance.
show that insurance was born of new contracts and markets rather than of mathematics.
explain how official suspicion of usury led merchants to invent the premium contract.

questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "the institution was invented by people who had no need of it. What they needed—and built—was a way of separating risk from credit, and a market…"

Why the other options fail:

  • (A) Strongest rival: true, but only part of the passage. P3 and P4 do say that pricing was social and stayed largely judgemental. But A leaves out the passage's central claim about origins: the premium contract that separated risk from credit (P2), restated in P5. A covers paragraphs 3–4, not the whole.
  • (B) Extreme. "The point is not that mathematics was irrelevant."
  • (D) Part for whole. Usury suspicion is one background factor in P2. The passage never says it caused the premium contract.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best expresses the contrast the author draws between grammar and punctuation?

options.html: Punctuation once marked grammatical structure but has come to serve chiefly as a guide to the rhythm of reading.
Both grammar and punctuation are conventions whose purpose is to prevent a reader from misconstruing a sentence.
Grammar governs speech while punctuation governs writing, so neither can be judged by the other's standards.
Grammatical regularities are followed without instruction, whereas punctuation conventions have to be learned.

questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: grammar "describes regularities that speakers follow whether or not they have been taught them"; punctuation is "learned rather than acquired".

Why the other options fail:

  • (A) Reversal of the history. The marks moved from rhythm to grammatical structure.
  • (B) Fusion or overgeneralisation. Preventing misreading is the purpose of punctuation conventions only. Grammar is described as regularities, not conventions.
  • (C) A neat symmetry the passage never draws. It isn't claimed that grammar governs speech only.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following would the author most likely advise a writer who is unsure whether to place a comma in a particular sentence?

options.html: Ask whether it spares readers a plausible misunderstanding without making the sentence clumsy, and otherwise keep to common practice.
Use it wherever a person reading the sentence aloud would naturally pause, since that was the mark's original purpose.
Use it only where an analysis of how the sentence's clauses relate shows it to be grammatically required.
Follow personal judgement, since no rule of punctuation carries any genuine authority.

questions.explanationHeading: Q10. Answer: A. Author would advise (moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence:

  • P4: "whether it forestalls a likely misreading at a tolerable cost in fluency".
  • P5: conventions have value, and a writer who uses "personal judgement alone" imposes costs.

A combines both points. It is phrased differently from the passage ("spares readers a plausible misunderstanding" = "forestalls a likely misreading"; "clumsy" = cost "in fluency").

Why the other options fail:

  • (B) The breath-pause side of the dispute. Only one of the two standards the author criticises.
  • (C) The grammatical side of the dispute. The other of the two standards.
  • (D) "Anarchy". P5 explicitly rejects it.

questions.stemHtml: With which of the following would the author be LEAST likely to agree?

options.html: Much of the disagreement about commas arises because the disputants invoke different standards.
A comma that departs from the standard rule is a mistake even if it causes no misreading.
Early punctuation marks were often added by people other than the person who wrote the text.
Idiosyncratic punctuation can impose costs on readers even when each individual choice is sensible.

questions.explanationHeading: Q11. Answer: B. LEAST likely to agree (moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Why B is the answer: B treats a departure from the rule as a mistake even when no misreading results. The author denies "rules of the kind either side imagines" and replaces "correct?" with "does it forestall misreading?". So the author would least agree with B.

The three options the author would accept:

  • (A) P3: "Each side appeals to a standard the other does not recognise."
  • (C) P2: marks were "added… by scribes, readers and later printers".
  • (D) P5: "however sensible each choice… that cost may exceed…"

Trap: a hasty reader may reason that because the author values convention, the author would call departures mistakes. But in the author's view the value of convention lies in cost to the reader. It does not make a departure an error.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that punctuation "enjoys no such grounding" as grammar does?

options.html: Style guides published in different countries continue to disagree about where commas belong.
Readers misconstrue sentences noticeably more often when the commas a grammatical analysis calls for are omitted.
Within a few decades of the arrival of printing, punctuation practice had become far more uniform.
People never taught punctuation, asked to mark divisions in unpunctuated text, reliably mark the same places.

questions.explanationHtml:
The target claim: grammar describes regularities "speakers follow whether or not they have been taught them", while punctuation "enjoys no such grounding… learned rather than acquired".

Why D: if untaught people reliably mark the same divisions in unpunctuated text, there is an untaught regularity behind punctuation. That is the very kind of grounding the author denies. D goes to the heart of the "learned rather than acquired" contrast.

Why the other options fail:

  • (A) Continued disagreement between style guides fits the author's picture of convention without a deeper basis. It supports the claim.
  • (B) Strongest trap. It shows that grammatically motivated commas reduce misreading. But that is the author's own practical account of punctuation, as a tool against misconstrual, and says nothing about untaught grounding. B is compatible with the claim.
  • (C) Standardisation by printers is a learned, institutional development. It supports "technology of the page".
questions.takeawayHtml: identify exactly what is being denied, here untaught grounding. The best underminer supplies evidence of that specific thing, not merely evidence that punctuation is useful.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following findings would most weaken the critics' objection described in the second paragraph, as applied to a particular behaviour?

options.html: Groups sharing one habitat and ancestry crack nuts differently, and an animal that switches groups adopts its new group's method.
A survey measuring far more environmental variables than earlier studies finds none that differs between the two populations.
A feeding technique seeded in a few trained birds spreads through their group and is still in use several seasons later.
The behaviour is present in one population and absent in another, although the two populations are genetically very similar.

questions.explanationHtml:
The objection: a behaviour that differs between groups "might reflect some feature of the habitat that researchers had simply failed to measure".

Why A:

  • The groups share one habitat and an ancestry, so no unmeasured habitat feature can separate them.
  • The individual who switches groups adopts its new group's method, which shows the method is learned socially.
  • A targets the objection for this behaviour, as the question stem requires.

Why the other options fail:

  • (B) Strong trap. Measuring more variables still leaves "another unmeasured variable… always available". The passage says such surveys strengthen the case "only a little".
  • (C) A seeding experiment. P4 says experimental evidence "does not automatically transfer" to the differences seen in the wild.
  • (D) Rules out genetics only. The critics' objection is ecological.
questions.takeawayHtml: a good weakener closes the specific gap the objection points to. Here that gap is an unmeasured habitat difference.

questions.stemHtml: It can be inferred that the author regards the seeding experiments as:

options.html: settling the older dispute, since social transmission can now be observed rather than merely inferred.
less informative than the method of elimination, because they depend on animals trained by researchers.
evidence that the differences between wild populations arose through social learning.
removing an objection in principle while leaving open how observed wild differences arose.

questions.category: RC: inference about the author's view
questions.explanationHeading: Q14. Answer: D. Inference about the author's view (moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: the experiments "remove the objection, made in advance of any evidence"; they do "not show that the differences observed between wild populations arose that way".

Why the other options fail:

  • (A) Contradicted: "a mistake… to treat these results as settling the older argument".
  • (B) Unsupported comparison. The passage never ranks the two methods' informativeness, and never criticises the use of trained animals.
  • (C) Contradicted: this is exactly what the experiments do not show.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following would the author regard as the strongest evidence for culture in the more demanding sense discussed in the final paragraph?

options.html: Birds that keep using their group's local feeding technique even after discovering an equally effective alternative.
A technique refined over generations into a form that naive animals, given the same materials, never reach.
A behaviour found in one population but not in a genetically similar one living in an identical habitat.
A technique invented by a single individual that spreads through the entire population within a single season.

questions.explanationHeading: Q15. Answer: B. Application to a concept (difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
The demanding sense of culture: a tradition "that accumulates… each generation building on the modifications of the last, so that the result exceeds what any individual could invent alone".

Why B: it shows refinement over generations and a result that naive individuals cannot reach alone. Both features of the definition are present.

Why the other options fail:

  • (A) Strongest trap. This is conformity to a local variant, which the passage cites in P3 as evidence of tradition. That is the weaker sense of culture.
  • (C) The method-of-elimination pattern, which bears on the weaker sense at most.
  • (D) Rapid spread is transmission, not accumulation.

questions.stemHtml: The author's attitude to the question of whether our own species is unique in possessing culture in the cumulative sense is best described as:

options.html: confident that it is unique, since cumulative traditions have not been demonstrated in any other species.
doubtful that the question is meaningful, since the answer depends wholly on how culture is defined.
undecided: evidence of cumulative traditions elsewhere is thin, yet not so thin as to show that we are unique.
persuaded that several species share culture in every sense of the word that matters.

questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "the evidence is far thinner… we do not yet know how unusual our own species is." The stem asks about culture in the cumulative sense. In the weaker sense, the author is not undecided: other species clearly have it.

Why the other options fail:

  • (A) Overreach. "Far thinner" is not the same as "none".
  • (B) Half-right. The answer does depend on definition, but the author calls the cumulative question "the more interesting question". That is not doubt about whether the question means anything.
  • (D) Extreme. The author says culture in the weaker sense only is "strong for a number of species".

questions.stemHtml: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4) below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in this sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.html: It is this indifference to posterity that makes the heap so valuable: it records habit rather than aspiration.
Archaeologists have long known that the richest record of a settlement is often its rubbish heap.
Hence a grave can tell us how a community wished its members to be remembered, while only the midden tells us what they actually ate.
What people threw away, unlike what they chose to bury with their dead, was never meant to be seen by anyone.

questions.explanationHtml:
The sequence:

  1. 2 opens. Rubbish heaps are rich records; "the heap" in 1 needs this.
  2. 4 contrasts discards with grave goods: "never meant to be seen".
  3. 1 "this indifference to posterity" refers to 4's "never meant to be seen". This is the heap's value: habit, not aspiration.
  4. 3 "Hence" draws the consequence of 1's habit/aspiration distinction: graves preserve remembrance, middens preserve diet.

Alternatives tested:

  • 2-3-4-1: "Hence" right after 2 has nothing to follow from. A heap being the richest record does not imply that a grave records remembrance. The order fails.
  • 2-4-3-1: "Hence" after 4 is possible. But then "this indifference" in 1 points back past 3, which says nothing about indifference. Inferior.
  • 4-2-…: 1 then needs "the heap" and "indifference" right behind it. No ordering allows that.

Audit note: the first draft of sentence 3 lacked "Hence", and the blind audit found 2341 equally coherent. Adding "Hence" fixed that by tying 3 to 1.

questions.stemHtml: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4) below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in this sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.html: The logic of collusion seems to doom them from the start.
The durable ones turn out to share a feature: some means by which members can observe one another's prices, so that undercutting is detected and punished before it pays.
Economists have long been puzzled less by why cartels collapse than by why some of them last.
Each member, after all, gains most by quietly undercutting the agreed price while the others hold to it.

questions.explanationHtml:
The sequence:

  1. 3 sets out the puzzle: why do some cartels last?
  2. 1 explains why lasting is puzzling. "Them" refers to cartels.
  3. 4 supplies the reason, signalled by "after all": each member's incentive to cheat.
  4. 2 resolves the puzzle: "The durable ones" share a monitoring feature.

Alternatives tested:

  • 1 cannot open, because "them" has no referent.
  • 2 placed right after 3 answers the puzzle before the paragraph has explained why it is a puzzle, and leaves 1 and 4 stranded.

questions.stemHtml: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4) below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in this sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.html: Jokes are said to be the hardest thing to translate, and the usual explanation is that they depend on wordplay.
Because none of this is on the page, a translator can render every word faithfully and still deliver a sentence that, to its new audience, is merely a sentence.
What they depend on instead is a shared stock of assumptions—about who is pompous, what is shameful, which situations are absurd—that the joke invokes without stating.
Yet many jokes that contain no pun at all still fail to cross a border.

questions.explanationHtml:
The sequence:

  1. 1 gives the usual explanation: wordplay.
  2. 4 "Yet" brings in a counterexample: jokes with no puns still fail.
  3. 3 "What they depend on instead" is the real dependence, unstated shared assumptions. "Instead" contrasts with wordplay.
  4. 2 "Because none of this is on the page" refers to 3's assumptions "without stating". It gives the consequence for translators.

Alternatives tested:

  • 1-2-4-3: in this position "none of this" would refer to wordplay. But wordplay is on the page, so 2 cannot follow 1.
  • 1-4-2-3: 2's "none of this" would point at puns that 4 has just said are absent, so the reference doesn't work.

The unique anchor is the link between 3's "without stating" and 2's "none of this is on the page".

questions.stemHtml: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4, 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.html: These benefits are real, but they are distributed by the same logic as most urban amenities: they accrue where trees already are.
A map of a city's canopy cover is thus, to a striking degree, a map of its past income.
Trees impose costs as well, since roots crack pavements and fallen leaves block drains, and these costs fall on municipal budgets.
City trees are usually justified by what they provide: shade, cooler streets, cleaner air, lower energy bills.
And trees already are, overwhelmingly, in the neighbourhoods that were wealthy when the planting was done, decades ago.

questions.explanationHtml:
The coherent paragraph is 4-1-5-2:

  1. 4 states the benefits.
  2. 1 "These benefits" accrue where trees already are.
  3. 5 "And trees already are" in neighbourhoods that were wealthy.
  4. 2 "thus" concludes: canopy maps past income.

Why 3 is odd: it stays on the topic of urban trees and even uses the paragraph's benefit/cost framing. But the paragraph's argument is about how benefits are distributed. Sentence 3 introduces costs to municipal budgets, which the chain never takes up.

It also cannot be inserted:

  • Placed after 4, it would make "These benefits" in 1 refer to costs.
  • Placed after 2, it would be a new argument tacked onto a conclusion.

You find the odd sentence by tracing the logical chain, not by spotting a topic shift.

questions.stemHtml: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4, 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.html: The reason, it seems, is that engines proved less a rival than an instrument, revealing in the games of the great players resources their contemporaries had missed.
Chess is not, in the technical sense, solved: no one knows whether perfect play from the opening position leads to a win or a draw.
When chess engines first surpassed the best human players, many expected the game to lose its appeal, as a solved puzzle loses its interest.
Masters now study engine lines the way musicians study recordings, not to imitate them but to hear what is possible.
The opposite happened: more people play chess now than at any earlier time.

questions.explanationHtml:
The coherent paragraph is 3-5-1-4:

  1. 3 states the expectation that the game would lose its appeal.
  2. 5 "The opposite happened."
  3. 1 "The reason" explains the paradox: engines became instruments.
  4. 4 illustrates how masters use engines.

Why 2 is odd: it is tightly linked to the wording of 3 ("a solved puzzle"), which is the trap. But it corrects a technical premise rather than advancing the argument about why interest rose.

It cannot be inserted:

  • After 3, it would separate the expectation from "The opposite happened".
  • Anywhere else, it interrupts the reason–illustration sequence.
questions.takeawayHtml: a sentence can share key words with the paragraph and still be odd. Ask whether it advances the paragraph's claim.

questions.stemHtml: The passage below is followed by four alternative summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
bodyHtml: Oral historians are sometimes asked to defend their sources against the charge of unreliability: memory is selective, reshaped by later events and coloured by the desire to present oneself well. The charge is true, but it mistakes what the sources are for. An interview recorded fifty years after a strike is poor evidence of what happened on the picket line on a given morning; written records usually do that better. It is excellent evidence of what the strike came to mean to those who lived through it, and of how that meaning was revised as their circumstances changed. The distortions that make memory unreliable as a record of events are, for this second purpose, the very data the historian is after.

options.html: Memory's distortions make oral testimony weak evidence of events but strong evidence of what events came to mean.
Oral history can match written records for reliability once the distortions introduced by memory have been identified and corrected.
Because memory is reshaped by later experience, oral testimony reveals more about the present than about the past.
Oral testimony is best used to fill the gaps that remain in the written record of events such as strikes.

questions.explanationHtml:
Why A: it keeps both halves. Memory is weak as evidence of events, and its distortions are themselves evidence of meaning.

Why the other options fail:

  • (B) Reversal. The distortions are data, not errors to be corrected.
  • (C) Overgeneralisation. The paragraph says testimony is evidence of meaning and its revision. It never claims testimony is "more about the present than the past". This is the closest trap.
  • (D) A role the paragraph doesn't give. It says written records are better for events.

questions.stemHtml: The passage below is followed by four alternative summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
bodyHtml: The patent system is usually defended as a bargain: the inventor receives a temporary monopoly, and in exchange the public receives a full description of the invention, which others may build on once the monopoly expires. The bargain depends on the description being useful. In practice, patent documents are drafted by lawyers whose aim is to claim as much as possible while revealing as little as necessary, and engineers in many industries report that they rarely read patents at all, except to check whether they are about to infringe one. If disclosure is the public's side of the bargain, the public may be receiving considerably less than the theory promises.

options.html: Because patent documents are drafted to conceal rather than to reveal, the patent system ought to be abolished.
Engineers avoid reading patents, since doing so exposes them to claims that they have infringed.
The usefulness of patent disclosure is undermined chiefly by engineers' reluctance to read patents.
The patent bargain assumes useful disclosure, but drafting practice and engineers' habits suggest the public gets less.

questions.explanationHtml:
Why D: it keeps the bargain, the condition (disclosure must be useful), the two pieces of evidence (drafting practice and engineers' habits) and the hedged conclusion ("may be receiving… less").

Why the other options fail:

  • (A) An extreme prescription. The paragraph gives no remedy.
  • (B) Causal distortion. Engineers read patents only to check for infringement. They don't avoid reading them because reading creates infringement exposure.
  • (C) Wrong cause. Engineers' habits are evidence of low usefulness. The paragraph locates the cause in drafting ("claim as much… revealing as little").

questions.stemHtml: The passage below is followed by four alternative summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
bodyHtml: It used to be assumed that sleep protects memory passively, by sparing the brain the interference of new experiences during the hours when it is offline. Experiments have since complicated that picture. Memories rehearsed during sleep—cued, for instance, by sounds or smells associated with the original learning—are retained better than memories that are not, and the improvement is selective, favouring material that the sleeper had been told would be useful later. Sleep, on this evidence, is not merely a period of reduced interference but an active process that sorts experience, strengthening what seems likely to matter.

options.html: Sleep protects memory by reducing interference, and cues presented during sleep reinforce this protective effect.
Sleep seems to strengthen memories selectively, favouring what may prove useful, rather than merely shielding them.
Because sounds and smells presented during sleep improve memory, new learning can evidently take place while we sleep.
Sleep strengthens all of the day's memories, and particularly those rehearsed through sensory cues linked to learning.

questions.explanationHtml:
Why B: it captures the change from passive protection to active, selective strengthening.

Why the other options fail:

  • (A) Keeps the old view that the paragraph revises.
  • (C) Scope shift. Cues strengthen material that was already learned. That is not new learning during sleep.
  • (D) "All of the day's memories" contradicts "selective".
