paragraphsHtml: Few historical theses have been demolished as thoroughly, or have survived as stubbornly, as the claim that childhood was invented. Its original proponent, a historian working largely from paintings, diaries and manuals of conduct, argued that medieval Europe had no concept of childhood as a distinct stage of life: once past infancy, children were dressed as small adults, mixed freely in adult work and play, and were mourned, when they died, with a restraint that later generations would find shocking. The modern sentiment of childhood—the conviction that children are fragile, innocent and in need of protected time—emerged, on this view, only in the early modern period.

The critics' case is now familiar. Medieval sources, read more widely, are full of toys, of laws treating children differently, of parents grieving extravagantly for the children they had lost. Painting is a poor guide to perception, because artistic conventions for depicting bodies change for reasons unrelated to how actual children were seen. And muted expressions of grief in a world of high infant mortality may say more about the genres in which grief was recorded than about the grief itself. Each objection is sound, and together they dispose of the thesis in its strong form: medieval people plainly knew that children were different, and they loved them.

What is less often noticed is that the critics answered a question the thesis did not most need to ask. Whether medieval parents loved their children is a question about sentiment, and sentiment is notoriously hard to read off from documents. The more defensible claim concerns institutions: the steady extension of the period of life during which a person is excluded from work and adult responsibility and placed instead in specialised settings—schools above all—organised around the idea that this period has a value of its own. That extension is not in dispute, and it is precisely the kind of change that can alter what childhood is, even if it does not alter how much children are loved.

Read this way, the original argument made two claims, one about feeling and one about arrangement, and presented them as though they were the same. Its critics showed the first to be false and assumed that they had thereby refuted the second. But a society can cherish its children while expecting them to herd animals at seven, and another can schedule every hour of a child's day around its development while being, in sentiment, no more tender. It is the arrangement, not the feeling, that has a history in the strong sense.

None of this rehabilitates the original evidence, much of which was as weak as the critics alleged. It suggests rather that a thesis can be wrong in the form its author gave it and right about something its author did not quite isolate—and that the refutation of the first does not, by itself, settle the second.
passages.notesTitle: Was childhood invented? (history; difficult)
passages.notesHtml:
How the passage is built:

  1. The thesis: medieval Europe had no concept of childhood; the modern sentiment of childhood arose in the early modern period.
  2. The critics: their objections are sound and refute the strong form of the thesis. Medieval people knew children were different, and loved them.
  3. The author's turn: the critics answered the wrong question. The defensible claim is institutional: the extension of a protected period of life spent in schools.
  4. The thesis conflated two claims, one about feeling and one about arrangement. The critics refuted the first and assumed they had refuted the second.
  5. The original evidence stays weak. A thesis can be wrong in its stated form yet right about something it did not isolate.

paragraphsHtml: When remote work became widespread, forecasts of the city's decline followed quickly. If the office was no longer necessary, the argument ran, neither was the expensive apartment within commuting distance of it, and the logic that had drawn people into dense centres for two centuries would run in reverse. The forecasts were not foolish, but they rested on a narrow account of what cities are for. They treated the city as a device for assembling workers in one place so that they could be supervised and coordinated—an account on which a technology that coordinates them at a distance does indeed make the city redundant.

Economists who study cities have long emphasised a different set of functions. Density makes it cheaper to find the right job, the right employee, the right supplier or the right collaborator, because the pool of candidates within reach is larger. It also accelerates learning: workers in large cities appear to acquire skills faster than comparable workers elsewhere, and they keep much of that advantage when they move away, which suggests that the city is not merely rewarding skills people already have but helping them acquire new ones. Neither function depends on a daily commute to a fixed desk. Both depend on a kind of unplanned proximity that video calls reproduce poorly, because calls are scheduled, bounded and confined to people one has already decided to talk to.

This suggests that remote work subtracts some of the city's functions more than others. It weakens the case for living near the office, but it leaves largely intact the case for living near other people who do what one does or would like to do. The effect should therefore fall unevenly. Established workers, whose networks are formed and whose skills are largely acquired, gain most from the freedom to leave. Younger workers, for whom the city's value lies chiefly in the learning and matching it provides, have the least reason to go—and some reason, as rents fall, to arrive.

If this is right, the likely outcome is neither the death of the city nor a return to the status quo, but a re-sorting of who lives there and why. Such a re-sorting could prove more disruptive than the forecasts of decline imagined, for a city whose population grows younger and more transient has different fiscal needs and a different political temper from one whose residents are rooted. Commercial districts built around daily commuters face a genuine crisis even in a city that is otherwise thriving.

The difficulty for anyone predicting what will happen is that the learning advantage of cities is easier to measure than to explain. If we knew precisely which kinds of encounter produce it, we could say which kinds remote work can replace. As it is, we know that density helps people learn; we do not know how much of that help can travel down a cable.
passages.notesTitle: Remote work and the city (urban economics; moderate)
passages.notesHtml:
How the passage is built:

  1. The forecasts of decline rest on a narrow view: the city as a place where workers are assembled and coordinated.
  2. Two other functions of cities, matching and learning, depend on unplanned proximity that video calls reproduce poorly.
  3. The effects will be uneven: established workers leave, younger workers stay or arrive.
  4. The result is a re-sorting, not a death. It may still be disruptive, and commercial districts face a crisis.
  5. The learning mechanism is not understood, so the prediction is uncertain.

paragraphsHtml: When a celebrated finding in psychology fails to replicate, two interpretations immediately present themselves. On the first, the original result was a false positive—an artefact of small samples, flexible analysis and the preference of journals for surprising claims—and the failure to replicate simply reveals that there was never anything there. On the second, the effect is real but fragile: it depends on conditions that the original study happened to satisfy and the replication did not, such as the population tested, the wording of instructions or the cultural moment. Defenders of a finding naturally prefer the second interpretation, and critics have learned to regard it with suspicion.

The suspicion is warranted, but not for the reason usually given. The objection to the "hidden moderator" defence is not that moderators are implausible. Most effects in psychology surely do depend on context; it would be strange if they did not. The objection is that a moderator invoked only after a replication has failed can rescue any finding whatever. Indeed, the more plausible a moderator sounds, the more tempting it is to invoke it after the fact, which is exactly why plausibility cannot be the test. If every failure can be attributed to some unspecified difference between studies, no failure counts against the claim, and a claim against which nothing can count has ceased to say anything about the world.

The remedy is not to forbid appeals to context but to require that they be made in advance. A researcher who states, before the replication, the conditions under which the effect should and should not appear has made a claim that the replication can test. If the effect then fails to appear under conditions the researcher said were favourable, the failure is informative in a way it could not otherwise be. Stated like this, the requirement is less a rule about replication than a rule about what it means to have made a claim in the first place.

It follows that much of the debate about whether particular findings are "real" is premature. Many original papers specified their effects so loosely that neither a successful nor a failed replication could bear on them very much. A successful replication of a vague claim confirms little, since a vague claim is compatible with many outcomes; a failed one refutes little, for the same reason. What the replication crisis has exposed, on this reading, is less a surplus of false findings than a shortage of precise ones.

This does not mean that every failed replication is uninformative. Where the original authors did specify their conditions, and the replication honoured them, failure is about as damning as evidence in this field gets. Where they did not, the most a failure can do is invite the authors to say, now and in advance, what their claim actually was. But the most important lesson may be prospective rather than retrospective: not which old findings to discard, but how new ones should be stated.
passages.notesTitle: What failed replications show (philosophy of science; difficult)
passages.notesHtml:
How the passage is built:

  1. Two interpretations of a failed replication: the original was a false positive, or the effect is fragile.
  2. The hidden-moderator defence is suspect. This is not because moderators are implausible, but because invoking them after the fact can rescue anything.
  3. The remedy: state conditions in advance. This is really a rule about what it is to make a claim.
  4. Vague claims can be neither confirmed nor refuted. The crisis shows a shortage of precise findings rather than a surplus of false ones.
  5. Some failures do count. The main lesson concerns how future findings are stated.

paragraphsHtml: For much of the twentieth century, the origin of farming was described as a revolution. Within a few centuries, on this account, foragers in a handful of regions began sowing and harvesting wild cereals, unwittingly selected plants whose seeds stayed on the stalk rather than scattering, and soon found themselves sedentary, numerous and dependent on crops that could no longer reproduce without human help. The word conveyed both speed and rupture: a before and an after, separated by a threshold that, once crossed, could not be recrossed.

Excavations over the past few decades have made the speed hard to sustain. Plant remains from sites in south-west Asia show people cultivating wild forms of cereals for a thousand years or more before the domestic, non-shattering forms came to dominate their harvests. Domestic traits appear first in small proportions and spread slowly, sometimes receding before advancing again. The pattern differs from region to region, and in some places domestic forms never came to dominate at all before cultivation was given up. At several sites, people seem to have farmed, abandoned farming and returned to it. If there was a threshold, it was approached by a long and wandering path.

Some revisionists have drawn the further conclusion that the idea of a revolution should be abandoned altogether—that what happened was not a transformation but a drift, a gradual adjustment of foraging practices with no decisive moment. This goes further than the evidence warrants. The slowness of the biological process tells us how long it took for crops to change. It does not tell us how quickly human societies changed once they had come to rely on those crops. The two timescales need not match. A dependence that was centuries in the making might nonetheless, once established, have reorganised settlement, labour, property and population within a few generations. Sedentary villages, once they exist, have a momentum of their own: they accumulate stores, invite raids, demand defence and make it harder for anyone to leave.

What the evidence actually requires, then, is a distinction between the process by which farming emerged and the consequences that followed from it. The process was slow, reversible and in many places tentative; there was no moment at which anyone decided to become a farmer. The consequences may well have been abrupt, and in that sense the older vocabulary captured something real, even if it misdated it. It is not that the older writers saw a sudden event where there was none; it is that they attached the suddenness to the wrong part of the story. A revolution need not be quick in its causes to be revolutionary in its effects.

The point is not merely terminological. If the consequences were abrupt while the process was slow, the people who lived through the change would have experienced it as sudden, whatever its long prehistory—much as a coastline that has been eroding for centuries can still collapse in a single storm.
passages.notesTitle: Was farming a revolution? (archaeology; moderate–difficult)
passages.notesHtml:
How the passage is built:

  1. The old account: a fast revolution.
  2. The evidence: domestication was slow, uneven and reversible.
  3. The revisionists over-infer. Biological slowness says nothing about the speed of social change, and settled villages have their own momentum.
  4. Distinguish the process from its consequences. The process was slow, but the consequences may have been abrupt. The old account was right about suddenness but attached it to the wrong part of the story.
  5. The change was experienced as sudden, as in the coastline analogy.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best describes the author's position on the thesis that childhood was invented?

options.html: The critics refuted it decisively by showing that medieval parents loved their children, and little of value survives.
It was largely correct, since the critics relied on sources no more trustworthy than the paintings it drew upon.
Its claim about feeling is refuted, but a claim about arrangements it conflated with that one survives.
Its central claim was always institutional, so the critics' objections about sentiment, though accurate, were beside the point.

questions.explanationHeading: Q1. Answer: C (author vs cited thesis; difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "the original argument made two claims, one about feeling and one about arrangement, and presented them as though they were the same. Its critics showed the first to be false…"

Why C is right: the thesis is refuted on feeling and survives on arrangement. "Conflated" corresponds to "presented them as though they were the same".

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (D) Strongest rival. It says the thesis's "central claim was always institutional", so the critics were "beside the point". But the author says the institutional claim is something the original author "did not quite isolate". It wasn't the thesis's central claim. The critics weren't beside the point either: they refuted the claim the thesis actually made.
  • (A) Contradicts "right about something its author did not quite isolate".
  • (B) A reversal. The author calls the critics' objections "sound" and the original evidence "as weak as the critics alleged".
questions.takeawayHtml: "the thesis was really about X" and "the thesis contained X without isolating it" are different claims. CAT distractors exploit exactly that gap.

questions.stemHtml: According to the author, the critics' reasoning went wrong because they took for granted that:

options.html: refuting the thesis about sentiment also refuted it about the arrangements of childhood.
medieval documents record faithfully how parents felt about the children they lost, whatever the genre.
paintings are a more reliable guide than written sources to how children were actually perceived.
the original historian had relied mainly on paintings rather than on the written evidence available.

questions.explanationHeading: Q2. Answer: A (critics' faulty assumption; difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "Its critics showed the first to be false and assumed that they had thereby refuted the second."

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) The critics argued the opposite: genres distort the recorded grief ("may say more about the genres…"). This assumption cannot be theirs.
  • (C) A reversal of the critics' view that "Painting is a poor guide to perception".
  • (D) True of the original historian, but it isn't an assumption in the critics' reasoning. It is a fact they used. True but irrelevant.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following would the author regard as the most relevant evidence for the version of the thesis that the author considers defensible?

options.html: Letters in which early modern parents express grief more intensely than medieval parents had done.
Records showing the typical age at which children began full-time work rising over several centuries.
Paintings in which children come gradually to be depicted with recognisably childlike proportions.
Medieval laws under which children were punished less severely than adults for the same offences.

questions.explanationHeading: Q3. Answer: B (relevant evidence across paragraphs; difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
The defensible claim: "the steady extension of the period of life during which a person is excluded from work". Rising ages for starting full-time work over centuries are direct evidence of that extension.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Evidence about sentiment, the claim the author says the critics refuted.
  • (C) Paintings, which "change for reasons unrelated to how actual children were seen". They are unreliable, and at most bear on perception.
  • (D) Strongest rival. Laws are institutions, which makes D tempting. But D shows only that medieval society treated children differently. That is the critics' evidence against the strong thesis. It says nothing about the extension over time of a protected period.
questions.takeawayHtml: match the evidence to the precise claim. Here the claim is about change over time in an arrangement, not the mere existence of an arrangement.

questions.stemHtml: The author's remark that a society "can cherish its children while expecting them to herd animals at seven" serves mainly to:

options.html: suggest that children in pre-modern societies were loved more deeply than children are today.
show that feelings about children and arrangements for them can vary independently.
imply that early work did no harm to children in societies that valued them.
concede that the critics were right that medieval children were treated as small adults.

questions.explanationHeading: Q4. Answer: B (purpose of an example; moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: the remark sits in a sentence pairing two hypothetical societies: one cherishes its children but sets them to work early; the other organises children's time but is "no more tender". The point is that sentiment and arrangement come apart.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) No comparison of how much children were loved is made.
  • (C) An unsupported value judgement.
  • (D) A misattribution. "Treated as small adults" is the thesis's claim, which the critics denied.

questions.stemHtml: The forecasts of urban decline described in the first paragraph depend on the assumption that:

options.html: remote work would be taken up by workers of every age and occupation in roughly equal measure.
video calls and similar tools can reproduce most of the benefits that unplanned proximity provides.
rents in city centres would fall sharply as soon as offices began to close.
people live in cities chiefly to be near the workplaces where their work is coordinated.

questions.category: RC: assumption of a cited argument
questions.explanationHeading: Q5. Answer: D (assumption of a cited argument; difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: the forecasts "treated the city as a device for assembling workers in one place so that they could be supervised and coordinated". D states this assumption.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Not needed. Decline could follow even if adoption were uneven.
  • (B) Strongest rival. It is tempting because the author criticises the forecasts for ignoring the benefits of proximity. But the forecasts didn't assume video replaces proximity. They simply didn't count proximity among the city's functions. Ignoring a factor and assuming a claim about it are different things.
  • (C) A possible consequence of the forecast, not an assumption behind it.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best describes the significance of the finding that city workers "keep much of that advantage when they move away"?

options.html: It proves that cities create skills rather than attracting workers who are already skilled.
It tells against the view that cities do no more than reward the skills that people bring to them.
It shows that the learning advantage of cities can be carried over in full to work done at a distance.
It suggests that workers who leave cities lose the skills acquired there more slowly than was expected.

questions.explanationHeading: Q6. Answer: B (inference with qualifiers; difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "which suggests that the city is not merely rewarding skills people already have but helping them acquire new ones."

Why B is right: "Tells against the view that cities do no more than reward" matches "not merely rewarding".

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Strongest rival. "Proves" is too strong, since the passage says only "suggests". "Rather than attracting" is an either/or the passage avoids: "not merely" allows that cities do both.
  • (C) A misreading. The finding concerns skills kept after moving away. It says nothing about whether the learning advantage can be delivered at a distance.
  • (D) An invented expectation ("more slowly than was expected").
questions.takeawayHtml: compare the force of each qualifier: suggests/proves, not merely/rather than.

questions.stemHtml: On the author's account, which of the following developments would be most surprising?

options.html: Workers early in their careers leaving big cities faster than established mid-career workers.
Commercial districts struggling badly in a city whose overall population is stable or even growing.
Falling rents drawing younger residents into large cities from which older residents are departing.
Workers with settled networks moving to smaller towns while keeping the jobs they already hold.

questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: younger workers "have the least reason to go", and established workers "gain most from the freedom to leave". If early-career workers left faster, the author's account would be contradicted.

Why the other options are wrong: B, C and D are each predicted in paragraphs 3–4. B: commercial districts "face a genuine crisis even in a city that is otherwise thriving". C: "some reason, as rents fall, to arrive". D: established workers gain "freedom to leave".

questions.stemHtml: The author's concluding remarks are best described as:

options.html: conceding that the case against the forecasts of decline cannot, in the end, be sustained.
suggesting that the learning advantage of cities has been overstated, since no one can explain it.
predicting that remote technologies will eventually reproduce the benefits that density provides.
acknowledging that the argument's prediction rests on a mechanism that is not yet understood.

questions.explanationHeading: Q8. Answer: D (function of the conclusion; moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "the learning advantage of cities is easier to measure than to explain… we do not know how much of that help can travel down a cable."

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Overreach. The author flags uncertainty but does not abandon the argument.
  • (B) A misreading. An advantage that is "easier to measure than to explain" is measured. Being hard to explain does not mean it is overstated.
  • (C) Unsupported. The author says we don't know.

questions.stemHtml: The author agrees with critics that the "hidden moderator" defence deserves suspicion, but differs from them in holding that:

options.html: moderators are seldom relevant to the kinds of effects that psychologists typically study.
appeals to moderators are legitimate only once the moderator has been shown to be independently plausible.
the fault lies in invoking moderators after the fact, not in their being unlikely.
most of the original findings were false positives produced by small samples and flexible analysis.

questions.explanationHeading: Q9. Answer: C (author vs critics; moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "The suspicion is warranted, but not for the reason usually given… not that moderators are implausible… a moderator invoked only after a replication has failed can rescue any finding."

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) A reversal. "Most effects… surely do depend on context."
  • (B) Close hedged trap. It sounds reasonable: allow moderators only when they are independently plausible. But the author says plausibility "cannot be the test", because "the more plausible a moderator sounds, the more tempting it is to invoke it after the fact". The test is timing: the moderator must be stated in advance.
  • (D) The author's own conclusion is "less a surplus of false findings".

questions.stemHtml: None of the following follows from the author's argument EXCEPT:

options.html: A failed replication of a loosely stated claim says little about whether it is true.
Replications should be attempted only where the original authors stated their conditions in advance.
Most celebrated findings in psychology will turn out, on closer inspection, to be false positives.
A successful replication of a precise claim is less informative than a failed replication of it.

questions.explanationHeading: Q10. Answer: A (double-negative inference; very difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
Decode the stem: exactly one option does follow from the argument.

Why A follows: "a failed one refutes little, for the same reason" (paragraph 4).

Why the other options don't follow:

  • (B) "Only" overreaches. The author says failures are most damning where conditions were specified. That doesn't mean other replications shouldn't be attempted. A failed replication can still prompt authors to "say… what their claim actually was".
  • (C) Contradicts "less a surplus of false findings".
  • (D) An unsupported comparison. The passage never ranks success against failure for precise claims. It discusses vague claims, where both are uninformative.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the replication crisis has exposed "less a surplus of false findings than a shortage of precise ones"?

options.html: Many replication attempts were carried out by researchers who were sceptical of the original findings.
Journals have recently begun to require researchers to register predicted moderators before collecting data.
Original studies in psychology have typically described their effects in vaguer terms than studies in other sciences.
Findings stated with precise, advance conditions failed faithful replications about as often as loosely stated ones.

questions.explanationHeading: Q11. Answer: D (weaken a comparative claim; very difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
The claim: the crisis reveals "less a surplus of false findings than a shortage of precise ones". In other words, imprecision explains the failures better than falsity does.

Why D weakens it: if precise findings with advance conditions fail faithful replications as often as vague ones, then imprecision isn't what explains the failures. The findings are simply false. That revives the "surplus of false findings" reading.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Sceptical replicators raise a separate worry about bias. It doesn't distinguish falsity from imprecision.
  • (B) About future reform. Irrelevant to what the crisis has exposed.
  • (C) Supports the author: psychology's claims are especially vague.
questions.takeawayHtml: to weaken "less X than Y", find evidence that Y (here, imprecision) doesn't explain the outcome.

questions.stemHtml: The author's statement that "a claim against which nothing can count has ceased to say anything about the world" is used to:

options.html: argue that claims about context-dependent effects are, by their nature, empty.
show that most findings in psychology cannot in practice be replicated.
explain why moderators invoked only after a failed replication are objectionable.
suggest that critics have been too quick to dismiss the results of failed replications.

questions.explanationHeading: Q12. Answer: C (purpose of a statement; moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: the line concludes the argument that "a moderator invoked only after a replication has failed can rescue any finding whatever."

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Overgeneralises. Context-dependent claims stated in advance are testable, which is the author's own remedy.
  • (B) A scope shift.
  • (D) A reversal. The author's point warns against dismissing failures too easily, not too quickly.

questions.stemHtml: The author's disagreement with the revisionists described in the third paragraph is best expressed as follows: the revisionists

options.html: overlook the evidence that domestic traits spread slowly and unevenly through early harvests.
infer the speed of social change from the slow pace of crop change.
place the beginning of cultivation much later than the surviving plant remains appear to suggest.
treat the dispute over the word "revolution" as though it were merely a matter of terminology.

questions.explanationHeading: Q13. Answer: B (author vs revisionists; difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "The slowness of the biological process tells us how long it took for crops to change. It does not tell us how quickly human societies changed."

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) A reversal. The revisionists rely on that very evidence.
  • (C) Invented. No dating dispute is described.
  • (D) A misreading. "Not merely terminological" is the author's point in the last paragraph, and isn't attributed to the revisionists.

questions.stemHtml: The comparison with an eroding coastline is intended to suggest that:

options.html: a change long in preparation may still be lived through as sudden.
a slow process cannot be recognised until it produces some visible and sudden result.
gradual change usually goes unnoticed by those who live through it.
abrupt events tend to be remembered afterwards as gradual ones.

questions.explanationHeading: Q14. Answer: A (purpose of an analogy; easy)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "the people who lived through the change would have experienced it as sudden, whatever its long prehistory."

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) Unsupported. The slow process (erosion) is plainly recognisable in the analogy. The point is about how the change is experienced, not whether it can be detected.
  • (C) A reversal. The point is that the change was felt.
  • (D) Invented claim about memory.

questions.stemHtml: It can be inferred that the author would accept which of the following?

options.html: The older account was right about the speed of domestication but mistaken about the consequences that followed.
Since farming was repeatedly abandoned and resumed, its social consequences cannot have been abrupt.
Societies that adopted farming slowly would have experienced the change as gradual, whatever its later effects.
Evidence of villages growing rapidly once crops became fully domestic would support the author's distinction.

questions.explanationHeading: Q15. Answer: D (inference across paragraphs; moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: the author's distinction predicts that consequences were rapid once dependence was established ("within a few generations", "momentum of their own"). Rapid village growth after full domestication is exactly what it predicts.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) A reversal. The old account was wrong about the speed of domestication and possibly right about its consequences.
  • (B) The revisionist inference the author rejects. Abandonment shows that the process was reversible, not that its consequences couldn't be abrupt.
  • (C) Hedged but contradicted. The final paragraph says the people who lived through the change would have experienced it as sudden "whatever its long prehistory". A slow process does not imply a gradual experience.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following most accurately states the author's view of the older account of farming as a revolution?

options.html: It correctly described both how farming emerged and what followed from it, apart from its dates.
It was wrong to call the change a revolution, although its dating of the change was broadly sound.
It may have described the effects of farming correctly while placing them at the wrong time.
It should be retained, because domestication proceeded faster than the revisionists suppose.

questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence:

  • "The consequences may well have been abrupt."
  • "The older vocabulary captured something real, even if it misdated it."
  • "They attached the suddenness to the wrong part of the story."

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Strongest rival. It says the old account described "both how farming emerged and what followed". But the old account was wrong about how farming emerged: it claimed speed where the process was slow. "Apart from its dates" hides that error.
  • (B) A reversal. The old account was right about the character of the change and wrong about its timing.
  • (D) Contradicts paragraph 2.
questions.takeawayHtml: keep the author's hedge. C's "may have" matches "may well have been". A claims far more than the author does.

sentences.html: The air in a given bubble is therefore younger than the ice around it, sometimes by centuries, and the two clocks must be reconciled.
As the snow is compressed it traps tiny bubbles of air, each a sample of the atmosphere of its year.
An ice core drilled from a glacier is a record of the atmosphere in the years when its snow fell.
Reading the record is not straightforward, however, because air goes on moving through the upper layers of snow for decades, and at some sites for centuries, before they seal.

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct order:

  1. 3 introduces the ice core as a record.
  2. 2 gives the mechanism: compressed snow traps bubbles.
  3. 4 adds a complication: "however", air keeps moving through the upper layers.
  4. 1 concludes: "therefore" the bubble is younger than the ice.

Why not other orders:

  • 1 needs both 2's bubbles and 4's mechanism before it. (Audit note: sentence 4 now says air moves "for decades, and at some sites for centuries", so it agrees with 1's "sometimes by centuries".)
  • 4's "the record" needs 3 before it.
  • 3-4-2-1 interrupts the complication with the basic mechanism.

sentences.html: Because a page or a monitor cannot reproduce such conditions, the best road-sign alphabets are tested not in studios but on test tracks, with drivers asked to read words as they approach.
Designers of road signs face a problem that designers of books do not: their text must be read at speed, at a distance and often at a glance.
Letters that are distinct on a page can merge at seventy metres, and a typeface that looks elegant on a monitor may blur in rain at night.
What matters, it turns out, is less the beauty of individual letters than the shape they make together—a word's outline, recognised before its letters can be resolved.

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct order:

  1. 2 states the problem: reading at speed, at distance, at a glance.
  2. 3 gives concrete failures: letters merge, typefaces blur.
  3. 1 "Because a page or a monitor cannot reproduce such conditions" introduces testing on tracks. "A page or a monitor" refers back to 3.
  4. 4 "What matters, it turns out" gives the finding from those tests.

Why not other orders:

  • 2-3-4-1 puts the finding ("it turns out") before the tests that produced it.
  • 2-1-3-4 fails because "a page or a monitor… such conditions" in 1 needs 3's page, monitor, seventy metres and rain.

Audit note: the blind re-audit flagged 2-1-3-4 as a weak rival. Sentence 1 was reworded to lock it to 3.

sentences.html: In the workshops of the early industrial era, absence on Mondays was so common that the day acquired a name of its own, as a kind of unofficial holiday.
The formal weekend, in other words, began less as a gift from employers than as a bargain struck with an existing habit.
Employers, unable to stamp out the practice, eventually found it cheaper to concede a half-day on Saturday in exchange for a full day's work on Monday.
Long before the two-day weekend was won by negotiation, many workers had taken it for themselves.

  2. 1 shows how: absence on Mondays.
  3. 3 gives the employers' response to "the practice".

questions.stemHtml: The passage below is followed by four alternative summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
bodyHtml: Defenders of zoos once justified them chiefly as places of education and recreation; the modern zoo justifies itself as an ark, breeding endangered species against the day they can be returned to the wild. The argument is strongest for the small number of species for which reintroduction has actually succeeded, and weakest for the large mammals that draw visitors, which breed poorly in captivity and for which suitable wild habitat may never again exist. The ark, in other words, may justify some of what zoos do far more than it justifies the zoos people actually visit.

options.html: The conservation rationale for zoos is persuasive for a few species but fits poorly with the large animals that make zoos popular.
Since large mammals breed poorly in captivity, zoos should give them up in favour of species that can be returned to the wild.
Zoos have exchanged education for conservation as their justification, and this has made them easier to defend.
The conservation work of zoos succeeds only with small species, which are not the ones that visitors come to see.

questions.explanationHtml:
Why A is right: it keeps the contrast: strongest for the few species successfully reintroduced, weakest for the big mammals that draw visitors.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (D) Strongest trap. It turns "a small number of species" into "small species". The paragraph's point is about how many species, not how big they are. "Succeeds only" also overstates "strongest for".
  • (B) A prescription the paragraph never makes.
  • (C) The paragraph never says zoos became easier to defend. It says the ark argument justifies "the zoos people actually visit" poorly.

questions.stemHtml: The passage below is followed by four alternative summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
bodyHtml: Fermentation is usually presented as a technique of preservation, and for much of history it was one: salting cabbage or souring milk kept food edible through winters that would otherwise have been hungry. But preservation does not explain why fermented foods remained central to cuisines long after refrigeration made them unnecessary. The likelier explanation is that fermentation, adopted for one reason, created flavours that people then came to value for their own sake, so that a practice of necessity became a practice of taste.

options.html: Fermentation survives mainly because its preserving function still matters wherever refrigeration remains scarce or costly.
Fermentation began as preservation but survives because the flavours it created came to be prized in themselves.
Now that refrigeration has made fermentation unnecessary, its continued use is a matter of habit rather than of need.
Fermented foods became central to cuisines because they kept food edible through winters that would otherwise have been hungry.

questions.explanationHtml:
Why B is right: it covers both the original function (preservation) and the reason the practice persists (taste valued for its own sake).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Wrong cause. The paragraph says fermented foods stayed central "long after refrigeration made them unnecessary", so their survival is explained by taste, not by a preserving function that persists where refrigeration is scarce.
  • (C) Close trap. "Habit" is not "taste". The paragraph says the flavours "came to be valued for their own sake".
  • (D) Covers only the first half of the paragraph.

questions.stemHtml: The passage below is followed by four alternative summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
bodyHtml: Surveys that ask people how satisfied they are with their lives produce answers that track income, health and relationships in the ways one would expect, which is reassuring evidence that they measure something real. Yet the same surveys show national averages that barely move over decades in which incomes have doubled. One reading is that people adapt to improvement, resetting their expectations as their circumstances rise. Another is that the scale itself shifts: a "seven out of ten" may mean something different to a richer generation. The two readings have very different implications, and the survey data alone cannot distinguish between them.

options.html: Satisfaction surveys capture something real, but their flat long-run averages fit two rival explanations that the data cannot tell apart.
Satisfaction surveys are unreliable, since their averages have failed to rise in step with incomes over several decades.
Because people adapt to improvements in their circumstances, rising incomes do not make populations more satisfied over time.
Since a given score may mean something different to a richer generation, flat averages probably conceal rising satisfaction.

questions.explanationHtml:
Why A is right: it keeps all three parts: the surveys measure something real, the long-run average is flat, and two readings remain that the data can't separate.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) Contradicts "measure something real".
  • (C) Adopts one reading as established.
  • (D) Hedged, but it still takes sides. "Probably conceal rising satisfaction" adopts the scale-shift reading. The paragraph says the data "cannot distinguish" between the readings, so even a hedged preference is unsupported.
questions.takeawayHtml: when a paragraph ends by saying the evidence "cannot distinguish" between readings, the correct summary must not pick one of them.
