paragraphsHtml: Most of what any of us knows, we know because someone told us. We have not measured the distance to the sun, witnessed the battles of the last century or tested the drugs we take; we have read, or heard, or been taught. The philosophical question is what entitles us to believe what we are told, and two answers have dominated the discussion.

The first, which may be called reductionist, holds that testimony is never a source of justification in its own right. We are entitled to accept what a speaker says only when we have independent reasons—a record of past reliability, say, or knowledge of the speaker's expertise—for thinking that speakers of that kind, on topics of that kind, tend to be right. The second view denies this. Testimony, it holds, is a basic source of knowledge, like perception or memory: we are entitled to accept what we are told by default, unless we have some positive reason to doubt it.

Each view has an embarrassment it cannot easily escape. The reductionist's independent reasons turn out, on inspection, to be shot through with testimony themselves. I believe that encyclopaedias are generally reliable because I have been told so, or because I have checked some of their claims against other sources that I accepted on someone's word. The inductive base from which testimony is supposed to be justified cannot be assembled without already relying on testimony. The default view, by contrast, makes justification too cheap. If I am entitled to believe whatever I am told unless I happen to have grounds for suspicion, then the credulous hearer, who never looks for such grounds, is as well justified as the careful one.

A more promising thought locates entitlement neither in the reasons the hearer possesses nor in a default the hearer enjoys, but in a disposition the hearer has. What distinguishes the careful listener from the credulous one is not that she has checked the speaker's credentials before every acceptance, which no one could do, but that she is responsive to signs that something is amiss—hesitation, implausibility, a conflict of interest, a claim that sits badly with what else she knows—and would withdraw her trust if they appeared. Her acceptance is not earned in advance; it is monitored as it goes.

Studies of young children lend this picture some support. Children accept a great deal of what adults tell them, which the reductionist would find hard to justify, since they have no general record of adults' reliability to draw on. But they do not accept it indiscriminately. Quite early, they prefer informants who have been accurate to informants who have erred, and they become wary of those who have something to gain from their belief. Their trust is generous, but it is not blind. If that is what testimonial entitlement looks like at its origin, it is neither earned nor free; it is held on condition.
passages.notesTitle: What entitles us to believe testimony? (epistemology; difficult)
passages.notesHtml:
Structure of the passage:

  • Reductionism: you need independent reasons to trust a speaker. Problem: those reasons themselves rest on testimony.
  • The default view: trust unless you have a reason to doubt. Problem: it makes the credulous hearer as justified as the careful one.
  • The author's view: entitlement is a disposition, meaning you are responsive to signs of unreliability. Trust is "monitored as it goes".
  • Children illustrate this: generous trust, but not blind trust. Trust is "held on condition".

paragraphsHtml: Museums are full of works their makers did not finish: canvases abandoned with a corner bare, statues whose figures seem to struggle out of the block, novels that stop mid-chapter. Many of them are among the most admired objects in their collections, and the admiration needs explaining. A finished work, after all, is what its maker intended; an unfinished one is, on the face of it, a work that failed to become what it was meant to be.

The usual explanation is documentary. The unfinished work, we are told, lets us see the artist at work—the underdrawing beneath the paint, the chisel marks that the polished surface would have erased—and so admits us to a process that completion conceals. There is truth in this, but it makes the appeal of the unfinished oddly second-hand. If what we value is evidence of process, then a well-preserved notebook or a film of the artist at work would serve as well or better, and the unfinished object would be merely a convenient source of information about something else. It would also leave unexplained why a sketch, which reveals process just as plainly, so often moves us less than an abandoned painting.

A second explanation locates the value in the viewer rather than the maker. Incompleteness, on this view, is an invitation: the bare corner and the half-emerged figure enlist the imagination in supplying what is missing, and the work is experienced not as a fixed object but as a field of possibilities. This is closer to what the encounter actually feels like, but it proves too much if left unqualified. A canvas with its lower half missing does not invite completion; it simply lacks something. What invites is a particular kind of incompleteness—one in which the parts that exist establish enough of a direction that the parts that do not can be imagined as continuations rather than guessed at as blanks.

There is also a historical complication. Our readiness to find unfinished works compelling owes a good deal to the art of the last century and a half, in which fragments, sketches and visible process became deliberate choices rather than accidents. Having learned to value incompleteness where it was intended, we have extended the same regard to works in which it was not. The admiration is genuine, but it is in part retrospective: we see in an abandoned Renaissance block an effect that its sculptor may have regarded only as a failure.

None of this makes the admiration mistaken. A work's meaning has never been confined to what its maker intended, and there is no reason why an effect that arose by accident should be less real than one that was planned. But it does suggest that "unfinished" names not a single aesthetic category but an intersection—of a particular structure in the object, a habit of attention in the viewer and a history that taught that habit. To ask whether an unfinished work succeeds is therefore to ask about all three at once.
passages.notesTitle: Why we admire unfinished works (aesthetics; moderate–difficult)
passages.notesHtml:
Structure of the passage:

  1. Documentary explanation. Problem: it is second-hand. A notebook or a film would serve as well, and a sketch would move us as much.
  2. Invitation explanation. It is closer to the experience, but needs a qualification: the existing parts must suggest how the missing ones continue.
  3. Historical complication. Modern art taught us to value incompleteness, and we now apply that value retrospectively.
  4. Conclusion. The admiration is not mistaken. "Unfinished" is an intersection of object, viewer and history.

paragraphsHtml: For a long time the standard account of metaphor treated it as a decoration. To call a man a lion was to say, in a heightened way, that he was brave, and the figure could in principle be replaced by its literal equivalent without loss of content, though with some loss of colour. The account fell out of favour for a good reason: the replacements never work. Any attempt to spell out what a rich metaphor means produces either a list that goes on indefinitely or a flat statement that misses what made the original worth saying.

The usual conclusion drawn from this failure is that metaphors carry a special kind of meaning—a metaphorical meaning, over and above the literal one, which resists paraphrase because it is not propositional in the ordinary way. This conclusion does not follow. That something cannot be paraphrased shows only that it is not a statement awaiting translation; it does not show that it is a statement of a stranger kind. A joke cannot be paraphrased either, and we do not infer that jokes have a secret "humorous meaning" that explanation fails to capture. We infer that what a joke does is not exhausted by what it says. The same reasoning would oblige us to posit a "musical meaning" for every melody that words fail to describe.

A more economical view holds that a metaphor means just what its words mean literally—usually something plainly false or absurd—and that its power lies in what this provokes. To be told that time is a thief is to be prompted to look at time in a certain light, to notice resemblances one had not attended to, and there is no determinate end to what such noticing may turn up. The open-endedness that defeated paraphrase is, on this view, not a feature of a hidden meaning but a feature of attention, which can always be extended further.

This view is right about living metaphors and wrong about what becomes of them. Language is full of expressions that began as figures and now carry literal senses of their own: we speak of the leg of a table, the mouth of a river, the branch of a bank, the face of a cliff, without provoking anyone to notice anything. These expressions mean what they mean because a metaphorical use, repeated often enough, hardened into a convention. If metaphors only ever meant what their words meant literally, it would be a mystery how they could leave new literal meanings behind.

The two observations can be reconciled. A living metaphor has no special meaning, but it has a career. Each use invites a way of seeing; when enough speakers accept the invitation in the same way, the way of seeing becomes a sense, and the figure dies into the dictionary. Metaphor, on this account, is not a second kind of meaning but one of the routes by which the first kind is made.
passages.notesTitle: What metaphors mean (philosophy of language; difficult)
passages.notesHtml:
Structure of the passage:

  1. Ornament view. Refuted: paraphrases always fail.
  2. Special-meaning view. It doesn't follow from that failure, as the joke and melody analogies show.
  3. Economical view. Literal meaning plus provoked attention. Right about living metaphors.
  4. But dead metaphors leave new literal senses behind, which the economical view can't explain.
  5. Reconciliation. Living metaphors have no special meaning but have a "career". Accepted ways of seeing harden into senses.

paragraphsHtml: Complaints about bureaucracy usually take the form of complaints about impersonality. The applicant who must fill in the same form as everyone else, whose circumstances are reduced to boxes and whose appeal is answered by a reference to the rules, experiences the office as a machine indifferent to the person standing in front of it. The complaint is old, and so is the classic reply: impersonality is not the defect of bureaucracy but its point. An official who treats every case by the same rule cannot favour a relative, punish an enemy or sell a decision to the highest bidder. What feels like coldness to the applicant is, from a wider vantage, a guarantee that strangers will be treated alike. Defenders of the system have long found that reply sufficient.

Both the complaint and the reply assume that impersonality is something an office either has or lacks, as though it were a property of its rules. It is better understood as an achievement, and a fragile one. Rules do not apply themselves. Every rule must be interpreted when it meets a case its authors did not foresee, and every official who interprets it brings to the task sympathies, suspicions and a sense of what the rule is for. The impersonal application of a rule is therefore not the absence of judgement but the discipline of judgement—the official's effort to set aside what she happens to feel about this applicant in favour of what any applicant in this position should receive.

That discipline is rarely complete. Studies of officials who deal directly with the public—caseworkers, inspectors, clerks at the counter—find that they routinely adapt the rules to the people before them, sometimes to help those they judge deserving, sometimes to protect themselves from those they find difficult. Much of this adaptation is invisible, because the official record shows only that the rule was applied. The office looks impersonal on paper while operating, at its edges, on something much closer to personal discretion. Officials themselves often describe these adjustments not as departures from the rules but as the only way of making the rules work.

The practical question, then, is not whether discretion should exist; it will exist whatever the rules say. The question is where it should sit and whether it can be seen. Discretion exercised openly, by officials required to record their reasons, can be reviewed and corrected, and its patterns can reveal where the rules themselves are failing. Discretion exercised covertly, under the appearance of mechanical application, escapes review precisely because it is denied.

This suggests an unexpected conclusion. The demand for strict impersonality, pressed too hard, may produce less of the equality it was meant to secure. An office forbidden to acknowledge judgement does not thereby eliminate it; it drives judgement into the places where no one can check it. Equality, on this view, is better served by judgement that is visible than by judgement that is forbidden.
passages.notesTitle: Bureaucracy and impersonality (social theory; moderate)
passages.notesHtml:
Structure of the passage:

  1. The complaint: bureaucracy is cold. The reply: impersonality guarantees equal treatment.
  2. Both are wrong to treat impersonality as a property of rules. It is a fragile achievement, "the discipline of judgement".
  3. In practice, officials adapt the rules invisibly.
  4. So the question is where discretion sits and whether it can be seen.
  5. Conclusion: strict impersonality can reduce equality by driving judgement out of sight.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best captures the position that the author finds most promising?

options.html: A hearer is entitled to accept testimony only once she has independent evidence that the speaker is reliable on the topic.
A hearer is entitled to accept testimony if she would notice and respond to signs of unreliability, though she has verified nothing beforehand.
A hearer is entitled to accept testimony by default, provided that at the moment of acceptance she has no positive reason for suspicion.
A hearer is entitled to accept testimony whenever the speaker lacks a conflict of interest and the claim fits what she already knows.

questions.category: RC: author's own view vs two cited views
questions.explanationHeading: Q1. Answer: B — author's own view (difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: The careful listener "is responsive to signs that something is amiss… and would withdraw her trust if they appeared. Her acceptance is not earned in advance."

Why B is right: B pairs a disposition to respond with no prior verification. Those are the two features the author names.

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) This is reductionism.
  • (C) The strongest rival. It describes the default view: having no reason for suspicion at the moment you accept. The author's view turns on whether you would respond if signs appeared, not on whether you happen to have none. The credulous hearer meets C's condition. That is exactly the author's objection.
  • (D) This turns some of the signs the passage lists into sufficient conditions. On the author's view the signs are things to stay alert to, not a checklist that grants entitlement.
questions.takeawayHtml: "Has no reason to doubt" (a state) and "would notice reasons to doubt" (a disposition) can look identical in an option. Telling them apart is the whole question.

questions.stemHtml: The author's objection to the second view would be most seriously weakened if it were shown that:

options.html: most speakers, on most occasions, sincerely report what they believe to be true.
careful hearers end up with a larger stock of true beliefs than credulous hearers do.
young children extend trust to adults long before they have any record of adults' accuracy.
only hearers who have searched for reasons to doubt can meet the condition of having none.

questions.explanationHeading: Q2. Answer: D — weaken the author's objection (very difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
The objection: On the default view, "the credulous hearer, who never looks for such grounds, is as well justified as the careful one."

Why D is right: The objection depends on the credulous hearer meeting the default condition (no reason to doubt) without ever having looked. Suppose only hearers who have searched for reasons to doubt can meet that condition. Then the credulous hearer fails it, the default view does separate careful hearers from credulous ones, and the objection loses its force.

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) That speakers are mostly sincere might make default trust pay off. It doesn't stop the default view ranking credulous and careful hearers equally.
  • (B) This supports the motive behind the objection: careful hearing matters.
  • (C) This concerns the reductionist's problem with children, not the default view.
questions.takeawayHtml: To weaken an objection, attack the premise it needs. Here that premise is that the credulous hearer qualifies.

questions.stemHtml: The author's remarks about encyclopaedias are intended to show that:

options.html: the first view's independent reasons cannot be gathered without relying on testimony.
encyclopaedias are considerably less reliable than the readers who consult them commonly assume.
the default view makes justification too easy, since readers rarely check what they read.
checking claims against further sources is the soundest way of justifying what one has been told.

questions.explanationHeading: Q3. Answer: A — purpose of an example (moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "The inductive base from which testimony is supposed to be justified cannot be assembled without already relying on testimony."

Why the others are wrong:

  • (B) The passage doesn't question how reliable encyclopaedias are.
  • (C) This misattributes the example. The encyclopaedia example targets reductionism. The "too easy" complaint is aimed at the default view, separately.
  • (D) This reverses the point: checking against other sources is itself testimony-dependent.

questions.stemHtml: The author cites studies of young children chiefly because their behaviour:

options.html: proves that testimony is a basic source of knowledge, on a par with perception and memory.
shows that children, like adults, base their trust on records of their informants' past accuracy.
suggests that trust in testimony is learned gradually through repeated experiences of being misled.
displays trust given without a track record yet withdrawn at signs of unreliability.

questions.explanationHeading: Q4. Answer: D — purpose of evidence (difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: Children "accept a great deal… since they have no general record of adults' reliability to draw on". "But they do not accept it indiscriminately… they become wary." "Their trust is generous, but it is not blind."

Why D is right: Generous-but-conditional trust is exactly the disposition view.

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Overstates. "Proves" is too strong, and the evidence is offered against the default view as much as for it ("not blind").
  • (B) The strongest rival. Children do prefer informants who have been accurate, a local and recent record. But the passage stresses that they trust widely without any general record of adults' reliability. B leaves out the generous half of the evidence and so recasts the children as reductionists.
  • (C) The passage never says trust is learned through being misled.

questions.stemHtml: The author's objection to the "documentary" explanation is that it:

options.html: exaggerates how much an unfinished work can reveal about the methods its maker used.
overlooks the fact that some artists left their works unfinished on purpose.
makes the object's appeal depend on information that other sources could supply as well.
confuses the process by which a work was made with the form it was meant to take.

questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "a well-preserved notebook or a film of the artist at work would serve as well or better".

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) The author never says the documentary view exaggerates what the work reveals.
  • (B) Deliberate incompleteness comes up only in the historical paragraph, as a point about modern art. It isn't the objection to this view.
  • (D) This is an invented confusion between process and intended form.

questions.stemHtml: The example of "a canvas with its lower half missing" is meant to show that:

options.html: incompleteness engages the imagination only when the existing parts suggest how the rest might go.
a large omission is more likely than a small one to stir the imagination of the viewer.
the second explanation is mistaken, since viewers do not in fact imagine missing parts.
physical loss and artistic incompleteness have much the same effect on the viewer.

questions.explanationHeading: Q6. Answer: A — purpose of an example (moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "What invites is a particular kind of incompleteness—one in which the parts that exist establish enough of a direction…"

Why the others are wrong:

  • (B) Reverses the point: the half-missing canvas fails to invite.
  • (C) Overreach. The author says the invitation view is "closer to what the encounter actually feels like". It is qualified, not rejected.
  • (D) Unsupported. The point is that mere lack differs from a suggestive gap.

questions.stemHtml: It can be inferred from the fourth paragraph that the author believes:

options.html: Renaissance sculptors often left their blocks unfinished in order to create a deliberate effect on viewers.
admiration for some older unfinished works draws partly on ways of looking learned from later art.
artists of the last century and a half valued incompleteness less than earlier artists did.
the admiration of unfinished older works is an error produced by reading history backwards.

questions.explanationHeading: Q7. Answer: B — inference with cross-paragraph check (difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "Our readiness… owes a good deal to the art of the last century and a half… The admiration is genuine, but it is in part retrospective."

Why the others are wrong:

  • (D) The strongest rival. "Retrospective" can sound like "anachronistic error". But the very next paragraph begins "None of this makes the admiration mistaken." You need both paragraphs to reject D.
  • (A) Contradicted: the sculptor "may have regarded [it] only as a failure".
  • (C) Reverses the passage. Modern art made incompleteness a deliberate choice.

questions.stemHtml: The author's concluding characterisation of "unfinished" implies that:

options.html: whether an unfinished work compels admiration cannot be settled by examining the object alone.
"unfinished" should be dropped as a category of criticism, since it names no single thing.
an unfinished work is compelling only if its maker intended the incompleteness.
the viewer's habits of attention matter more than the structure of the object itself.

questions.explanationHeading: Q8. Answer: A — implication of the conclusion (difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "'unfinished' names… an intersection—of a particular structure in the object, a habit of attention in the viewer and a history that taught that habit." "To ask whether an unfinished work succeeds is therefore to ask about all three at once."

Why A is right: If the answer depends on three factors, examining the object alone can't settle it.

Why the others are wrong:

  • (B) Overreach. The author redescribes the category but doesn't drop it.
  • (C) Contradicted: "there is no reason why an effect that arose by accident should be less real".
  • (D) An unsupported ranking. The three factors are presented together; none is said to matter more.

questions.stemHtml: The author uses the comparison with jokes in order to argue that:

options.html: metaphors, like jokes, tend to lose their force once someone attempts to explain them.
jokes and metaphors both carry meanings that no explanation can fully capture.
metaphor is best understood as a species of verbal humour.
a metaphor's resistance to paraphrase does not show that it carries a special meaning.

questions.explanationHeading: Q9. Answer: D — purpose of an analogy (moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "That something cannot be paraphrased shows only that it is not a statement awaiting translation… A joke cannot be paraphrased either, and we do not infer that jokes have a secret 'humorous meaning'."

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) The strongest rival. Jokes and metaphors may well lose their force when explained, but that isn't what the analogy is used to argue. Its job is to block an inference: "cannot be paraphrased, therefore it has a special meaning".
  • (B) Reverses the analogy's point.
  • (C) Absurd overextension.

questions.stemHtml: The author's main reservation about the view described in the third paragraph is that it:

options.html: underestimates how open-ended the effects of a living metaphor can be.
wrongly holds that living metaphors mean only what their words literally mean.
cannot explain how repeated figurative uses come to leave behind new literal senses.
treats metaphors as ornaments that could in principle be replaced by literal statements.

questions.explanationHeading: Q10. Answer: C — author vs cited view (difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "This view is right about living metaphors and wrong about what becomes of them… it would be a mystery how they could leave new literal meanings behind."

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Reverses the view. The economical view is the one that emphasises open-endedness.
  • (B) The author agrees with this part ("right about living metaphors").
  • (D) This is the ornament view from paragraph 1, not the economical view.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following would the author regard as the clearest example of a metaphor that has "died into the dictionary"?

options.html: A poet describing hope as "the thing with feathers" in a poem about despair.
A hiker referring to the "foot" of a mountain with no thought of a body.
A manager calling a difficult colleague "a volcano" to make the others laugh.
A scientist describing the brain as "a computer" in order to suggest new hypotheses.

questions.explanationHtml:
Why B is right: "The foot of a mountain", used "with no thought of a body", parallels "the leg of a table… without provoking anyone to notice anything".

Why the others are wrong: A, C and D are each living uses, chosen to provoke a way of seeing: a poem, a joke and a heuristic.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best expresses the reconciliation proposed in the final paragraph?

options.html: A live metaphor means just what its words say; shared ways of seeing can become senses.
Metaphors have a special meaning while alive, and this meaning becomes literal when they die.
Metaphorical and literal meaning are two kinds of meaning that shape each other over time.
Only dead metaphors carry meaning, since living ones provoke attention rather than state anything.

questions.explanationHeading: Q12. Answer: A — synthesis of the conclusion (difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "A living metaphor has no special meaning, but it has a career… when enough speakers accept the invitation in the same way, the way of seeing becomes a sense." The wording of A differs from the passage: "means just what its words say" for "no special meaning", and "shared ways of seeing can become senses" for "when enough speakers accept the invitation in the same way, the way of seeing becomes a sense".

Why the others are wrong:

  • (B) The strongest rival. It sounds like the "career" story, but it gives living metaphors a special meaning, which the author denies.
  • (C) Contradicted: "not a second kind of meaning".
  • (D) Misreads the passage. Living metaphors do carry meaning: their ordinary literal meaning.

questions.stemHtml: The author's disagreement with both "the complaint and the reply" concerns:

options.html: whether the impersonal application of rules really protects applicants from favouritism.
whether applicants are right to experience bureaucratic procedures as cold and indifferent.
their shared assumption that impersonality resides in rules rather than in officials' efforts.
whether officials ought to be permitted to interpret the rules they apply at all.

questions.category: RC: author vs both cited views
questions.explanationHeading: Q13. Answer: C — author vs both cited views (moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "Both the complaint and the reply assume that impersonality is something an office either has or lacks, as though it were a property of its rules. It is better understood as an achievement."

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) The author never disputes that impersonality protects against favouritism.
  • (B) How applicants experience bureaucracy is not the point of disagreement.
  • (D) The author says interpretation is unavoidable. Whether it should be permitted never arises.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's concluding claim?

options.html: Officials say that they depart from the rules mainly in order to help applicants they consider deserving.
Applicants tend to rate offices with strict rules as fairer than offices that allow discretion.
In the great majority of cases, officials interpret the rules they apply without any difficulty.
Similar applicants were treated more alike where officials recorded reasons for departures than where departures were banned.

questions.explanationHtml:
The conclusion: demanding strict impersonality "may produce less of the equality it was meant to secure". Equality is "better served by judgement that is visible".

Why D is right: If similar applicants are treated more alike where reasons are recorded than where departures are banned, that is direct evidence for the conclusion.

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Officials' stated motives don't bear on whether banning discretion reduces equality.
  • (B) Applicants' perceptions of fairness aren't measures of equal treatment. If anything, B points the other way.
  • (C) This weakens a premise: if interpretation is rarely difficult, there is little hidden discretion to worry about.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following can be inferred about the "official record" mentioned in the third paragraph?

options.html: It is deliberately falsified by officials who wish to conceal favouritism toward applicants.
It can make an office's practice look more uniform than that practice really is.
It provides the main evidence on which studies of officials' adaptations have relied.
It shows that, in most cases, the rules are in fact applied mechanically and uniformly.

questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "the official record shows only that the rule was applied. The office looks impersonal on paper."

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Extreme: the passage says nothing about deliberate falsification.
  • (C) Contradicted. The adaptations are "invisible" in the record, so the studies must rely on other sources.
  • (D) Misreads the passage. The record shows mechanical application; it doesn't prove that application happened.

questions.stemHtml: The phrase "the discipline of judgement" suggests that impersonal treatment:

options.html: requires that officials who depart from the rules be punished for doing so.
leaves no room for an official's judgement once the rules are properly written.
demands that officials restrain their own reactions while still interpreting the rules.
depends on judgement being taught as rigorously as the skills of any profession.

questions.explanationHeading: Q16. Answer: C — phrase in context (easy)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "not the absence of judgement but the discipline of judgement—the official's effort to set aside what she happens to feel".

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Plays on the punitive sense of "discipline".
  • (B) Contradicted: rules must always be interpreted.
  • (D) Takes "discipline" in the sense of a field of study. The passage never says this.

questions.stemHtml: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4) below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in this sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.html: Imitating admired predecessors was, accordingly, not a confession of weakness but the ordinary path to mastery.
Only when the artist came to be seen as the source, rather than the transmitter, of what a work expressed did novelty become a virtue in its own right.
For centuries, a painter or poet was praised for handling an inherited subject well, not for inventing a new one.
The demand that a work of art be original is younger than we tend to assume.

questions.explanationHtml:
Order:

  1. Sentence 4 makes the claim: the demand for originality is recent.
  2. Sentence 3 supports it: for centuries, artists were praised for handling inherited subjects.
  3. Sentence 1 follows with "Imitating… was, accordingly, the ordinary path". "Accordingly" depends on 3's norm.
  4. Sentence 2 closes with "Only when… did novelty become a virtue". This explains how the modern demand arose.

Alternative orders rejected:

  • 4-1-3-2: "Accordingly" right after 4 would draw imitation from the bare claim about dates. It has nothing to follow from.
  • 4-3-2-1: This ends on the old norm after the modern turn has already been explained. That breaks the movement from past to present.

questions.stemHtml: The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4) below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order of the sentences and key in this sequence of four numbers as your answer.

sentences.html: Quantification, on this view, is less a sign of confidence than a substitute for it—the method of those whose personal judgement would not be believed.
Numbers enjoy a peculiar authority in public life.
That appearance is most valuable precisely where trust is weakest: an official who cannot rely on the deference of the public can still rely on a calculation.
A figure seems to speak for itself, free of the interests of whoever produced it.

questions.explanationHtml:
Order:

  1. Sentence 2 introduces the authority of numbers.
  2. Sentence 4 explains why: a figure "seems to speak for itself".
  3. Sentence 3 follows with "That appearance", which refers to 4's "seems". It is most valuable where trust is weak.
  4. Sentence 1 concludes with "on this view": quantification is a substitute for confidence.

Locked links:

  • 3 needs 4 for "That appearance" to refer back to.
  • 1 needs 3's point about trust for "on this view".

questions.stemHtml: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4, 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.html: To generalise—to recognise that this dog, like others, may bite—one must let go of what made each earlier dog distinct.
What we tend to forget first, studies suggest, is the general pattern, while vivid particulars persist.
Forgetting, on this view, is not the enemy of learning but one of its instruments.
Forgetting is usually treated as a failure of memory, a leak in a system designed to retain.
Yet a memory that kept everything would be nearly useless, since every new situation would summon a flood of irrelevant particulars.

questions.explanationHtml:
The coherent paragraph is 4-5-1-3:

  1. Sentence 4: forgetting is treated as a failure.
  2. Sentence 5: "Yet" a total memory would be useless.
  3. Sentence 1: generalising requires letting go of particulars.
  4. Sentence 3: "on this view" forgetting is an instrument of learning.

Why 2 is odd: It shares the topic and the key word. But it contradicts the paragraph's central step. Sentence 1 says generalising requires letting go of particulars, so forgetting serves learning by discarding particulars and keeping the pattern. Sentence 2 says the opposite happens: we lose the pattern first and keep vivid particulars.

It can't be inserted anywhere. Placed after 4, it would be offered in support of the failure view, but then 5's "Yet… nearly useless" and 1's mechanism directly contradict it.

Audit note: the first draft's odd sentence (the shape of the forgetting curve) could be eliminated just by noticing a change of aspect, so it was replaced with one that you have to argue away.

questions.stemHtml: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4, 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.html: Its length is specified as exactly as any note's, and a performer who shortens it changes the piece as surely as one who plays a wrong pitch.
Composers have long exploited this, placing silences where the music has created a demand that it then withholds.
Because a rest contains no sound, performers are free to treat its length as a matter of taste.
A rest in a musical score is not an absence of music but a part of it.
What the listener hears in a rest is shaped by what came before and by what is expected next: a silence after a questioning phrase is heard as waiting.

questions.explanationHtml:
The coherent paragraph is 4-1-5-2:

  1. Sentence 4: a rest is part of the music.
  2. Sentence 1: "Its length" is specified exactly.
  3. Sentence 5: what the listener hears in a rest depends on context.
  4. Sentence 2: composers have "exploited this".

Why 3 is odd: It shares the topic and the vocabulary (rest, length, performers), but it contradicts the paragraph. Sentence 1 says changing a rest's length "changes the piece", while 3 says its length is "a matter of taste". Sentence 3 also contradicts 4, which says a rest is "not an absence of music".
questions.takeawayHtml: When every sentence is on topic, look for the one that conflicts with a premise.

questions.stemHtml: The passage below is followed by four alternative summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
bodyHtml: Talk of national character has a bad reputation, and deservedly: it has licensed stereotypes, justified exclusions and explained away injustice as temperament. But the reaction against it has sometimes gone too far, denying that the institutions and histories of different societies leave any lasting mark on how their members behave. Surveys and experiments find persistent differences between countries in, for example, how readily strangers are trusted—differences that track historical experience and outlast migration by a generation or more. The error of the old talk was not to see such differences but to treat them as fixed essences rather than as the sediment of circumstance.

options.html: Societies' histories do leave lasting differences in behaviour, but as the residue of circumstance, not as fixed essences.
Persistent differences in trust between countries vindicate the older idea of national character, if not its political uses.
Because talk of national character has excused injustice, the idea of lasting differences between societies should be rejected.
The behavioural differences produced by a society's history largely disappear within a generation of migration.

questions.explanationHtml:
Why A is right: It keeps both halves of the paragraph. Lasting differences are real (against the overreaction), and they are circumstantial, not essences (against the old talk).

Why the others are wrong:

  • (B) The strongest trap. "Vindicate the older idea" ignores the author's point that the old idea's error was treating differences as essences. Only the observation of differences is vindicated, not the idea.
  • (C) This is the overreaction the author criticises.
  • (D) Contradicted: the differences "outlast migration by a generation or more".

questions.stemHtml: The passage below is followed by four alternative summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
bodyHtml: The finding that the average of many independent guesses is often more accurate than the guess of any single expert is sometimes taken to show that expertise is overrated. It shows something narrower. Averaging works because individual errors, if they are independent, tend to cancel, and this requires that the guessers know enough for their errors to be scattered around the truth rather than piled up on one side of it. A crowd of people who share the same misconception will average to the same misconception. The crowd's wisdom, in other words, depends on a distribution of partial knowledge; it is a way of pooling expertise, not of doing without it.

options.html: Crowds are more accurate than experts, provided that their members do not all share the same misconceptions.
The accuracy of averaged guesses shows that expertise is overrated, except where crowds share a misconception.
Experts should be preferred to crowds whenever a misconception is likely to be widely held.
Averaging guesses works only when partial knowledge scatters errors around the truth, so it pools expertise.

questions.explanationHtml:
Why D is right: It keeps the condition (errors scattered around the truth require partial knowledge) and the conclusion (crowds pool expertise, they don't replace it).

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Keeps "more accurate than experts" as a general claim and adds a single exception. It misses the main point: the crowd depends on distributed knowledge.
  • (B) Keeps the inference "expertise is overrated", which the author rejects.
  • (C) A prescription the paragraph never makes.

questions.stemHtml: There is a sentence missing from the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and decide where (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence fits best.
questions.insertSentenceHtml: Print changed this by making every copy of an edition identical, page for page.
questions.placementParagraphHtml: Before the printed book, an index was of limited use, because two copies of the same text rarely shared the same pagination. ___(1)___ A reference to a passage had to name a chapter or a verse, or rely on the reader's familiarity with the text. ___(2)___ For the first time, a page number meant the same thing in every copy. ___(3)___ Readers could now be sent directly to a passage they had never read, in a book they had never opened. ___(4)___ The index thus encouraged a new way of reading: not from beginning to end, but by consultation, extracting what one needed and leaving the rest.

options.html: Option 1
Option 2
Option 3
Option 4

questions.explanationHeading: Q23. Answer: B, gap 2 — sentence placement (moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
The sentence: "Print changed this by making every copy… identical." "This" must refer to the problem of mismatched pagination and chapter-or-verse references.

Gap Verdict
1 Locally plausible, because the problem has just been stated. But the next sentence ("A reference… had to name a chapter") is still about the world before print, so placing the sentence here breaks the chronology.
2 Correct. The problem is complete, and the next sentence ("For the first time…") states the consequence of identical copies.
3 Comes after the consequence. It would explain the cause after the effect, and "this" would have no clear referent.
4 Too late.

questions.stemHtml: There is a sentence missing from the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and decide where (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence fits best.
questions.insertSentenceHtml: Introduce a mismatch between the forecast and the sensation, and the dampening should weaken.
questions.placementParagraphHtml: Most people cannot tickle themselves, and the reason seems to lie in prediction. ___(1)___ When we move, the brain generates a forecast of the sensations the movement will cause, and sensations that match the forecast are dampened. ___(2)___ A self-produced touch is therefore felt less intensely than the same touch delivered by someone else. ___(3)___ In experiments in which a robot inserted a small delay between a person's movement and the resulting touch, the touch began to tickle, and the longer the delay, the more it did. ___(4)___

options.html: Option 1
Option 2
Option 3
Option 4

questions.explanationHeading: Q24. Answer: C, gap 3 — sentence placement (moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
The sentence: "Introduce a mismatch… and the dampening should weaken." This is a prediction, so it belongs between the theory and the experiment that tests it.

Gap Verdict
1 No forecast has been described yet.
2 Locally plausible, because the dampening has just been mentioned. But it would break the link between "dampened" and the next sentence, which begins "A self-produced touch is therefore…".
3 Correct. Theory, then prediction ("should"), then the delay experiment that confirms it.
4 It would state the prediction after the result. "Should" no longer fits there.
