paragraphsHtml: Why should a court today be bound by what another court decided fifty years ago? The question is more awkward than it looks. If the earlier decision was right, the present court would presumably reach the same result on its own; if it was wrong, following it merely repeats the error. On either branch, precedent seems to add nothing except the possibility of perpetuating mistakes, and its authority appears to rest on little more than the accident of which case happened to arrive first.

The standard defences point to values that correctness alone cannot secure. People arrange their affairs—sign contracts, buy property, plan businesses—in reliance on the law as it has been declared, and a rule that may be overturned at any time is a poor foundation for such plans. Treating like cases alike is also a requirement of fairness: two litigants with indistinguishable claims should not receive different answers merely because they appeared before different judges or in different decades. And a system in which every question could be reopened in every case would be ruinously slow. Predictability also constrains judges themselves, making it harder for a court to decide a case according to the sympathies of the moment.

These defences are sound, but they do not apply with equal force everywhere. Reliance matters most where people actually rely: on the rules governing commercial transactions or the transfer of land, where the content of the rule often matters less than its being settled and known. It matters least where no one could reasonably have planned around the rule, and where the cost of an error falls on people who had no say in it. A precedent that misreads the scope of a basic liberty is not made more tolerable by the fact that institutions have grown accustomed to it. The strength of precedent should therefore vary with the kind of question it settles—strongest where settledness is the main good, weakest where it is the error itself that endures.

Courts rarely say anything so explicit. They have instead developed the technique of distinguishing: a precedent is not overruled but confined to its facts, the present case being declared different in some respect that makes the earlier reasoning inapplicable. Distinguishing allows the law to change while preserving the appearance of continuity, and in moderation it is a reasonable way of testing an old rule against circumstances its authors did not foresee. Used without restraint, it produces a different problem. Each distinction adds an exception, each exception invites further argument about its boundaries, and a body of law that was once simple becomes a thicket that only specialists can navigate.

The irony is that a technique meant to protect the value of predictability can end by destroying it. A rule riddled with distinctions may be formally intact and practically unknowable—binding in name, but no longer able to tell anyone in advance what they may do.
passages.notesTitle: Precedent (law; hardest)
passages.notesHtml:
How the passage is built:

  1. The puzzle. If a precedent was right, the court would reach the same result anyway; if wrong, following it repeats the error.
  2. The standard defences. Reliance, treating like cases alike, efficiency and constraint on judges.
  3. The author's thesis. These defences vary by domain. Precedent should be strongest where being settled is the main good, and weakest where the error itself endures, as with basic liberties.
  4. Distinguishing. Courts use it instead of explicit overruling. In moderation it is reasonable; unrestrained, it produces a thicket.
  5. The irony. Distinguishing can destroy the predictability it was meant to protect.

paragraphsHtml: Arguments about recommendation algorithms usually turn on diversity. Critics charge that systems which suggest what to watch, read or listen to next confine users to ever-narrower versions of what they already like, so that taste contracts into a feedback loop. Defenders reply that the evidence is mixed at best: many users encounter a wider range of material than they did when choice was limited to what a local shop happened to stock, and some systems deliberately inject novelty to keep users from growing bored. Each side can cite studies, and the studies are hard to compare, since they define diversity in different ways.

Both sides measure the same thing—the variety of what people consume—and it is not obvious that this is the right measure. Taste is not an inventory. A person with a vast collection of recordings may have very little taste, and a person who has heard only a few may have a great deal. What we mean by taste is closer to a capacity: the ability to discriminate, to say why one thing is better than another, to recognise quality in an unfamiliar form. And that capacity appears to be formed less by exposure than by a particular kind of experience—choosing for oneself, being disappointed, and working out what went wrong.

Recommendation systems are designed to reduce exactly that experience. Their measure of success is that the user is satisfied with the next item and stays for the one after. A system that worked perfectly would never disappoint, and in never disappointing it would deprive the user of the occasions on which judgement is exercised and refined. Disappointment, on this account, is not a defect in the experience of choosing but its most instructive part. The result need not be narrower consumption. It could be broad consumption by people progressively less able to say what they think of any of it.

It might be objected that taste has always been guided. Critics, booksellers and knowledgeable friends steered people towards some works and away from others long before any algorithm did. The difference lies less in the fact of guidance than in its form. A critic gives reasons, and reasons can be disputed; one can read a review, disagree with it and, in the course of disagreeing, discover what one values. A recommendation gives no reasons beyond the bare fact of a correlation—people who liked this also liked that—and offers nothing to argue with.

None of this requires that the systems be abandoned. It suggests rather that their designers have been answering the wrong question. Whether users see enough variety is a question about what passes before them. Whether they are becoming better judges of it is a question about what happens in them, and it is the second that the old intermediaries, for all their snobberies, at least attempted to address. That question is harder to measure, which may be why it is so rarely asked.
passages.notesTitle: Recommendation and taste (technology and society; moderate)
passages.notesHtml:
How the passage is built:

  1. The debate is about diversity. Critics say recommendations narrow what people consume; defenders say they widen it.
  2. The author's turn: taste is a capacity to discriminate, not an inventory. It is formed by choosing, being disappointed and reflecting.
  3. Recommendation systems remove disappointment, so consumption could be broad while judgement weakens.
  4. The objection that taste was always guided. Critics gave reasons that could be disputed; algorithms give correlations with nothing to argue against.
  5. The designers ask the wrong question: variety, when they should be asking whether users become better judges.

paragraphsHtml: The history of public health has long been told as a story of knowledge triumphing over superstition. Physicians in the mid-nineteenth century, so the story runs, believed that disease arose from miasma—foul air rising from rotting matter—until the germ theory replaced their error with truth, and mortality fell as a result. The new history under review sets out to dismantle this account, and much of its demolition is persuasive.

Its central exhibit is chronology. In many cities, deaths from waterborne disease began to decline well before germ theory won acceptance among physicians, let alone officials. The decline followed the construction of sewers, the paving of streets and the provision of piped water—works undertaken largely by reformers who believed in miasma. Cities that built sewers early saw cholera and typhoid recede, while cities that delayed continued to suffer, whatever their physicians believed. The author's point is that a mistaken theory produced the right interventions: if bad smells cause disease, then removing filth removes the smells, and removing filth also, as it happens, removes the bacteria. The reformers were wrong about why their measures worked, and the measures worked anyway.

So far, so instructive. The difficulty arises when the author moves from this case to a general moral, suggesting that the history of medicine shows theory to matter much less than practice, and that the achievements usually credited to scientific understanding were more often the fruit of practical trial and error. The argument proves less than it claims. A wrong theory produces right interventions only when its recommendations happen to coincide with those a true theory would make, and the book's own evidence shows how fragile that coincidence was. The same conviction that smells were the danger led some authorities to flush sewage into rivers, removing the stench from the streets while delivering the contamination to the drinking water downstream. Where miasma and germs pointed in the same direction, the reformers prospered; where they diverged, the theory killed people.

What the episode actually suggests is that practice can outrun understanding for a while, but only on credit. A practice grounded in a false theory succeeds by luck of alignment, and it has no way of knowing when its luck will run out. A sanitarian who did not know why clean water mattered could not know which of his measures to keep when money ran short. Germ theory did not merely ratify what the sanitarians had already achieved; it explained why their successes were successes and their failures failures, and so made it possible to keep the one and stop the other.

This is a substantial and often brilliant book, and its revision of the triumphalist narrative will stand. Its account of the sanitary movement, in particular, deserves to become the standard one. It would have been more brilliant still had its author resisted the temptation to replace one simple story with its mirror image.
passages.notesTitle: Book review on public health and theory (moderate)
passages.notesHtml:
How the passage is built:

  1. The triumphalist story: germ theory replaced miasma, and mortality fell.
  2. The book's chronology: mortality fell first, through sanitation carried out by believers in miasma. A wrong theory produced the right interventions.
  3. The reviewer's objection: the book over-generalises that theory matters little. Wrong theories work only where their advice happens to match the truth. Flushing sewage into rivers shows what happens where the two diverge.
  4. Practice can outrun understanding "only on credit". Germ theory explained which measures to keep.
  5. Verdict: a brilliant book that replaces one simple story with its mirror image.

paragraphsHtml: Projects that aim to return land to a wilder state face a question that sounds simple and is not: wild as of when? A wetland drained two centuries ago, a forest cleared before records began, a grassland shaped for millennia by grazing animals that have since disappeared—each could be restored to a different past, and each past would produce a different landscape. The choice of a baseline determines what counts as success, and there is no obviously correct one to choose.

Part of the difficulty is psychological. Ecologists have described a tendency for each generation to treat the condition of nature in its own youth as the normal state of affairs, against which later losses are measured. A fisherman who remembers the catches of his first years at sea regards them as the baseline, unaware that his predecessors would have considered them evidence of a depleted sea. Over several generations, the standard of what is natural drifts downward without anyone noticing. The same drift has been documented for birds, wildflowers and the size of trees.

One response is to reach back as far as possible, to a state before people altered the land at all. But in many regions there is no such state within reach of reconstruction, and even where there is, the climate, soils and surrounding landscape have changed so much that the old community of species could not persist. Even the attempt to reconstruct such a state depends on fragmentary evidence—pollen, bones, old accounts—that can support several pictures at once. Restoring a list of species that lived somewhere ten thousand years ago may require continual intervention to maintain—a garden, in effect, labelled as wilderness.

A more promising approach shifts attention from composition to process. Instead of specifying which species should be present at the end, it asks which processes should be allowed to operate: grazing by large herbivores, the flooding of rivers, the spread of natural disturbance, the movement of predators. Where the original grazers are extinct, hardy cattle or horses may be brought in to do their work, since it is the grazing, not the grazer, that matters. Restore those, the argument runs, and the landscape will find its own form, which may resemble no particular past at all. The goal is not a picture but a set of dynamics.

The approach has its own weakness. A goal defined by processes is harder to evaluate than one defined by species, because almost any outcome can be described as the result of processes having been allowed to operate. Without some account of which outcomes would count as failure, a process-based project risks becoming successful by definition, whatever happens. The answer is probably a compromise: processes as the goal, with a small number of indicators—the return of certain species, the recovery of soil or water quality—treated not as targets but as warning lights.
passages.notesTitle: Rewilding and baselines (ecology; easiest)
passages.notesHtml:
How the passage is built:

  1. Which past? The choice of baseline determines what counts as success.
  2. Shifting baselines: each generation's idea of what is normal drifts down.
  3. Pre-human baselines often can't be reconstructed or sustained, which gives "a garden… labelled as wilderness".
  4. The process approach: restore processes such as grazing and flooding, not lists of species. The grazing matters more than the grazer.
  5. The weakness: the approach risks being successful by definition. The compromise is to use indicators as warning lights.

questions.stemHtml: The passage below is followed by four alternative summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
bodyHtml: Online retailers offer free shipping not because delivery has become costless but because customers respond to a price of zero differently from any other price. A charge of even a small amount prompts shoppers to weigh whether the purchase is worth it; its removal eliminates that moment of deliberation altogether. Retailers recover the cost through higher prices or minimum order sizes, which customers notice far less. Free shipping, in other words, is less a discount than a way of moving a cost to where it will not be felt.

options.html: Because delivery has become much cheaper, retailers can now offer it free without raising the prices of their goods.
Free shipping works by moving delivery costs to where they prompt less deliberation, not by abolishing them.
Customers favour free shipping because they tend to overestimate what delivery actually costs retailers.
Free shipping is a genuine discount, which retailers fund by accepting a lower profit on each order.

questions.explanationHtml:
Why B is right: It captures the mechanism, a price of zero removing the moment of deliberation. It also keeps the conclusion that the cost is moved, not removed.

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Contradicted: the paragraph says it is "not because delivery has become costless".
  • (C) Gives an invented cause. Nothing is said about customers overestimating costs.
  • (D) Contradicted: "less a discount", and the cost is recovered through prices.

questions.stemHtml: There is a sentence missing from the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and decide where (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence fits best.
questions.insertSentenceHtml: Even then, few people expected the requirement to outlast the conflict.
questions.placementParagraphHtml: For most of history, travellers crossed borders without any document proving who they were. ___(1)___ Passes and letters of safe conduct existed, but they were requests for protection addressed to foreign authorities, not proofs of identity. ___(2)___ The modern passport, with its photograph and standardised format, is largely a product of the First World War, when states anxious about spies and deserters began demanding that every traveller be identifiable. ___(3)___ Yet measures introduced as temporary wartime controls survived the peace and were standardised by international agreement in the 1920s. ___(4)___ The document we now treat as a natural feature of travel is, in other words, an emergency measure that was never repealed.

options.html: Option 1
Option 2
Option 3
Option 4

questions.explanationHeading: Q2. Answer: C, gap 3 (sentence placement; moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
What the sentence needs: "Even then, few people expected the requirement to outlast the conflict." So it needs an introduced requirement and a conflict, "then" must refer to a time, and it should come before the surprise that the requirement survived.

Gap Verdict
1 No requirement or conflict has been introduced yet.
2 Still describes the old letters of safe conduct, so "the requirement" has no referent.
3 Correct. It follows the wartime demand and sets up the next sentence, "Yet measures introduced as temporary… survived the peace."
4 Locally plausible, because the topic is still the requirement. But the requirement has already outlasted the war, so a sentence saying few expected it to outlast the conflict comes too late.

questions.stemHtml: According to the author, the strength of a precedent should depend chiefly on:

options.html: whether settledness or correctness is the greater good for the kind of question it decides.
how long it has stood and how far institutions have adjusted their practices to it.
whether the court that decided it ranks above the court now asked to follow it.
how closely the facts of the present case resemble the facts of the earlier one.

questions.explanationHeading: Q3. Answer: A (principle the author proposes; difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "The strength of precedent should therefore vary with the kind of question it settles—strongest where settledness is the main good, weakest where it is the error itself that endures."

Why the others are wrong:

  • (B) This is the strongest rival. It treats institutional adjustment as the measure, but the author explicitly rejects that for basic liberties: "not made more tolerable by the fact that institutions have grown accustomed to it."
  • (C) Court hierarchy is never discussed.
  • (D) Factual similarity is what distinguishing turns on. It is not the author's criterion for strength.

questions.stemHtml: Each of the following pairs a consideration discussed in the passage with the kind of rule to which, on the author's view, that consideration applies with special force, EXCEPT:

options.html: reliance — rules governing the transfer of land
institutions' reliance — precedents that misread the scope of a basic liberty
the cost of an enduring error — rules whose errors fall on people who had no say in them
the value of settledness — rules governing commercial transactions

questions.explanationHeading: Q4. Answer: B (odd pair out; difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
How to read the question: check each pair. Does the author say this consideration applies with special force to this kind of rule?

Pair Does the author support it?
(A) Reliance and land transfer Yes: "Reliance matters most… on the rules governing… the transfer of land"
(B) Institutions' reliance and precedents misreading a basic liberty No. The author says the opposite: such a precedent "is not made more tolerable by the fact that institutions have grown accustomed to it"
(C) The cost of an enduring error and rules whose errors fall on people with no say Yes: reliance "matters least… where the cost of an error falls on people who had no say in it". There, precedent is "weakest", because "the error itself… endures"
(D) Settledness and commercial rules Yes: there "the content of the rule often matters less than its being settled"
questions.takeawayHtml: in pairing questions, check both halves of every pair. The odd pair often reuses a word from a correct pair (here, "reliance") and attaches it to the wrong domain.

questions.stemHtml: It can be inferred that the author regards the technique of distinguishing as:

options.html: a dishonest device by which courts overrule precedents while refusing to admit it.
the most effective means available to courts of keeping the law predictable.
a reasonable way to test old rules that becomes self-defeating when overused.
a practice that ought to give way to explicit overruling whenever a precedent is doubted.

questions.category: RC: inference about the author's attitude
questions.explanationHeading: Q5. Answer: C (inference about the author's attitude; moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "in moderation it is a reasonable way of testing an old rule… Used without restraint, it produces a different problem."

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Calling distinguishing "dishonest" goes too far. The author calls it "reasonable" in moderation, and preserving "the appearance of continuity" is a description, not an accusation.
  • (B) Reverses the irony in the last paragraph.
  • (D) The author never prescribes explicit overruling "whenever a precedent is doubted".

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument of the third paragraph?

options.html: Commercial parties generally prefer a clear rule that is imperfect to an uncertain rule that is correct.
People routinely plan around precedents on basic liberties and lose much when these are overturned.
Precedents concerning basic liberties have historically been overturned less often than commercial ones.
Judges frequently disagree about which questions concern basic liberties and which do not.

questions.explanationHtml:
The argument being weakened: reliance "matters least where no one could reasonably have planned around the rule". The example given is precedents on basic liberties.

Why B weakens it: if people routinely plan around precedents on basic liberties and lose a great deal when those precedents are overturned, then reliance does matter there. That undercuts the premise behind varying precedent's strength.

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Supports the paragraph's point about commercial rules.
  • (C) How often such precedents are overturned is a descriptive fact. It says nothing about how strong they should be.
  • (D) This is the closest rival. If judges disagree about what counts as a basic liberty, the principle becomes harder to apply, but its premise is untouched. B attacks the premise directly, so it weakens the argument more.

questions.stemHtml: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4, 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.html: The container replaced all this with a single standard box that could move from truck to ship to train without being opened, cutting a ship's time in port from days to hours.
Loading times barely changed, but containers reduced theft so sharply that insurance costs fell.
Before the shipping container, loading a cargo ship meant handling thousands of separate items—sacks, barrels, crates—each lifted and stowed by hand.
The cost of moving goods across oceans fell so far that it ceased to be a major consideration in deciding where things should be made.
A vessel could spend as long in port being loaded as it spent at sea.

questions.explanationHtml:
The coherent paragraph is 3-5-1-4:

  1. Sentence 3: cargo was once handled by hand.
  2. Sentence 5: a ship could spend as long in port as at sea.
  3. Sentence 1: the container replaced all this, cutting time in port from days to hours.
  4. Sentence 4: the cost of shipping fell so far it no longer shaped decisions about where to make things.

Why 2 is odd: It is on the same topic, containers and costs, but it contradicts sentence 1. Sentence 1 says time in port fell "from days to hours"; sentence 2 says "loading times barely changed". It also leaves 5's problem (long port times) without the solution that 1 supplies.

You eliminate it by finding the contradiction, not by spotting a change of topic.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best describes what the author finds lacking in the arguments of both the critics and the defenders?

options.html: Both ignore the evidence that some systems deliberately inject novelty into what they recommend.
Both exaggerate how far users' consumption has narrowed since such systems became widespread.
Both assume that algorithms can explain the reasons behind the items that they recommend.
Both judge the systems by what users consume, not how users learn to judge.

questions.explanationHeading: Q8. Answer: D (author vs both sides; moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "Both sides measure the same thing—the variety of what people consume—and it is not obvious that this is the right measure."

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) The defenders cite the injection of novelty.
  • (B) Applies to the critics only, and the author doesn't judge whether they exaggerate.
  • (C) Neither side is said to assume that algorithms give reasons.

questions.stemHtml: The statement that "Taste is not an inventory" implies that taste is wrongly thought of as:

options.html: a fixed set of likings that experience can do little to change.
a record of preferences that a system can store, analyse and then predict.
an assessment of quality carried out by experts on behalf of everyone else.
a stock of things encountered rather than an ability that has been developed.

questions.explanationHeading: Q9. Answer: D (phrase in context; moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "Taste is not an inventory… What we mean by taste is closer to a capacity."

Why D is right: The contrast in the passage is between a stock or collection and an ability.

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Nothing is said about taste being unchangeable.
  • (B) This is the closest trap. It sounds algorithmic, but the passage contrasts collecting with capacity, not storable records with something unpredictable.
  • (C) Describes what critics do, not what taste is mistaken for.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following changes to a recommendation system would the author most likely regard as addressing "the right question"?

options.html: Raising the share of unfamiliar items in what each user is shown.
Attaching to each suggestion a short, disputable case for why it deserves attention.
Letting users rate each recommendation so that the system learns their tastes faster.
Recommending only items that a panel of respected critics has already approved.

questions.explanationHeading: Q10. Answer: B (application to a hypothetical change; moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
The "right question": whether users "are becoming better judges". The author says reasons that can be disputed help with this: "one can read a review, disagree with it and… discover what one values."

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Variety is explicitly "the wrong question".
  • (C) Learning tastes faster serves user satisfaction, the very thing that removes disappointment.
  • (D) This is the strongest rival. Critics' approval is still guidance without reasons given to the user. It leaves "nothing to argue with".

questions.stemHtml: The passage suggests each of the following about traditional intermediaries such as critics EXCEPT that they:

options.html: steered people towards some works and away from others.
offered judgements that a reader could dispute.
were free of the prejudices that distort algorithmic recommendations.
tried, at least, to make people better judges of what they encountered.

questions.explanationHtml:
Why C is the exception: The passage says the old intermediaries had "snobberies". It never says algorithms are distorted by prejudice, and it never says critics were free of it.

What the passage does suggest:

  • (A) They "steered people towards some works and away from others".
  • (B) "Reasons can be disputed".
  • (D) They "at least attempted to address" whether people became better judges.

questions.stemHtml: The passage below is followed by four alternative summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
bodyHtml: When a language loses its last speakers, linguists often console themselves that it has at least been documented: recorded, transcribed, described in a grammar. Documentation preserves a great deal, but it preserves the language as an object rather than as a practice. A grammar can tell a future reader how sentences were formed; it cannot tell them what it was like to joke, quarrel or console in that language, or which expressions carried weight in which company. What survives is something like a skeleton: complete in its structure and accurate in its proportions, and lacking precisely what made it alive.

options.html: Documenting a dying language preserves its structure but not the lived practice of speaking it.
Documentation preserves a language accurately, which is why linguists are right to find it consoling.
Grammars of dying languages fail to record how their sentences were formed.
A documented language survives more completely than its last speakers tend to believe.

questions.explanationHtml:
Why A is right: It keeps the structure-versus-practice contrast, which the skeleton metaphor makes vivid.

Why the others are wrong:

  • (B) This is the closest trap. It accepts the linguists' consolation and leaves out the paragraph's point that what made the language alive is lost.
  • (C) Contradicted: a grammar "can tell a future reader how sentences were formed".
  • (D) The claim about what speakers believe is invented.

questions.stemHtml: There is a sentence missing from the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and decide where (1, 2, 3 or 4) the missing sentence fits best.
questions.insertSentenceHtml: The distinction matters because the public tends to hear such a probability as if it were a date.
questions.placementParagraphHtml: Seismologists distinguish between predicting an earthquake and forecasting one. ___(1)___ A prediction names a time, a place and a magnitude: a large quake will strike this fault next Tuesday. ___(2)___ A forecast states a probability over a long period: there is a one-in-three chance of a major quake in this region within thirty years. ___(3)___ Predictions in this strict sense have never been reliably achieved, and many seismologists doubt they ever will be. ___(4)___ Forecasts, by contrast, are routine, and they are what building codes and insurance premiums are based on.

options.html: Option 1
Option 2
Option 3
Option 4

questions.explanationHeading: Q13. Answer: C, gap 3 (sentence placement; moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
What the sentence needs: "The distinction matters because the public tends to hear such a probability as if it were a date." It needs the probabilistic forecast example ("a one-in-three chance… within thirty years") immediately before it. The "date" picks up the prediction ("next Tuesday").

Gap Verdict
1 Locally plausible, since "the distinction" picks up "distinguish". But "such a probability" has no antecedent yet.
2 Follows the prediction example, which gives a date, not a probability.
3 Correct. It follows the forecast's probability directly.
4 "Such a probability" is now two sentences back, and the insertion would separate "Forecasts, by contrast" from the sentence about predictions that it contrasts with.

Audit note: the first draft ("hear the second as if it were the first") fitted equally well at gap 1. The sentence was rewritten to tie it to the forecast example.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best expresses the reviewer's assessment of the book?

options.html: Its chronology is mistaken, since germ theory was widely accepted before mortality began to fall.
It rightly shows sanitation preceding germ theory, but draws too sweeping a moral from it.
It demonstrates that practical trial and error, not understanding, has been the engine of medical progress.
It underrates the reformers, whose belief that foul air caused disease was largely correct.

questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "much of its demolition is persuasive… The argument proves less than it claims… replace one simple story with its mirror image."

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) The reviewer accepts the chronology.
  • (C) This is the book's moral, which the reviewer rejects.
  • (D) The reviewer never calls miasma theory "largely correct". The theory was wrong, and its measures worked anyway.

questions.stemHtml: The reviewer mentions authorities who flushed sewage into rivers in order to:

options.html: show that the false theory worked only where its advice matched a true one's.
suggest that the reformers cared rather less about public health than the book claims.
explain why germ theory came to be accepted once miasma theory had failed.
cast doubt on the book's account of when deaths from waterborne disease declined.

questions.explanationHeading: Q15. Answer: A (purpose of an example; moderate)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "Where miasma and germs pointed in the same direction, the reformers prospered; where they diverged, the theory killed people."

Why the others are wrong:

  • (B) The reformers' motives are never questioned.
  • (C) The passage doesn't explain why germ theory came to be accepted.
  • (D) The chronology isn't doubted.

questions.stemHtml: The reviewer's remark that practice can outrun understanding "only on credit" suggests that:

options.html: successful practice will in time generate the understanding that is needed to justify it.
no practice can succeed unless a correct theory has first explained it.
practitioners who lack understanding should be granted only limited authority.
practice built on a false theory relies on luck that may end without warning.

questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "A practice grounded in a false theory succeeds by luck of alignment, and it has no way of knowing when its luck will run out."

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Unsupported. Practice doesn't generate understanding by itself; germ theory had to supply it.
  • (B) Contradicted: the sanitarians' practice succeeded without a correct theory.
  • (C) A literal-minded misreading of "credit".

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following, if discovered, would the reviewer regard as most consistent with the argument of the fourth paragraph?

options.html: A treatment discovered by trial and error that has never been explained and has never once failed.
A theory accepted on strong evidence that recommended no change at all in existing practice.
A traditional remedy that cured one illness but harmed a similar one until its working was explained.
A correct theory that was ignored for decades while practitioners carried on as before.

questions.category: RC: application to a new case
questions.explanationHeading: Q17. Answer: C (application to a new case; difficult)
questions.explanationHtml:
What the fourth paragraph describes: a practice that works by luck of alignment and fails where its theory diverges from the truth, until a correct explanation sorts its successes from its failures.

Why C is right: A remedy that helps with one illness but harms with a similar one, until its working is explained, has the same structure.

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) This is the strongest rival. An unexplained treatment that has never failed is compatible with the argument, but it doesn't display the argument's key feature: luck running out where theory and truth diverge.
  • (B) A correct theory that recommends no change in practice doesn't bear on the argument.
  • (D) Neglect of a correct theory is a different phenomenon.

questions.stemHtml: Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4, 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in its number as your answer.

sentences.html: A passer-by could take the vegetables and pay nothing, and no one would ever know.
Part of the explanation seems to be that people pay not to avoid detection but to remain, in their own eyes, the kind of person who pays.
Those who take without paying, however, are usually caught by cameras that farmers install after the first losses.
Farm stalls that leave produce by the roadside with a box for payment depend on a kind of trust that economists once found hard to explain.
Yet most people pay, and studies of such stalls find that losses are usually small enough to be absorbed.

questions.explanationHtml:
The coherent paragraph is 4-1-5-2:

  1. Sentence 4: honesty stalls depend on trust that is hard to explain.
  2. Sentence 1: no one would ever know if you didn't pay.
  3. Sentence 5: "Yet" most people pay.
  4. Sentence 2: they pay to stay, in their own eyes, the kind of person who pays, not to avoid detection.

Why 3 is odd: It shares the topic, but it contradicts two premises. Sentence 1 says "no one would ever know"; sentence 3 says non-payers are "usually caught by cameras". Sentence 3 also undercuts 2's explanation that detection is beside the point.

questions.stemHtml: The example of the fisherman illustrates:

options.html: how fishermen tend to exaggerate the size of the catches they took in earlier years.
why the condition of an ecosystem in the distant past can never be reconstructed.
why fish catches have declined steadily over the course of several generations.
how each generation's idea of normal can quietly lower the standard for judging loss.

questions.explanationHeading: Q19. Answer: D (purpose of an example; easy)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "the standard of what is natural drifts downward without anyone noticing."

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Reverses the example. The fisherman underestimates past abundance.
  • (B) Wrong paragraph and wrong claim.
  • (C) No cause of decline is given.

questions.stemHtml: The phrase "a garden, in effect, labelled as wilderness" describes:

options.html: a restored landscape that can be kept as it is only by continual human management.
a landscape that looks wild but has been stocked with species introduced from elsewhere.
a protected area that visitors are not permitted to enter.
a restoration project that has failed to attract the particular species it was designed for.

questions.explanationHeading: Q20. Answer: A (phrase in context; easy)
questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "may require continual intervention to maintain—a garden, in effect, labelled as wilderness."

Why the others are wrong:

  • (B) This is the closest trap. Introducing substitute animals is discussed in paragraph 4, as part of the process approach, and with approval. The garden phrase is about the need for continual intervention.
  • (C) Visitor access is never mentioned.
  • (D) Nothing is said about a project failing to attract species.

questions.stemHtml: The author's view of the process-based approach is best described as:

options.html: dismissive, since almost any outcome can be described as a success under it.
enthusiastic, since it guarantees landscapes resembling some genuine past state.
favourable but qualified: it needs some means of recognising failure.
favourable, chiefly because its results are easier to evaluate than those of other approaches.

questions.explanationHtml:
Evidence: "A more promising approach…", "The approach has its own weakness…", "The answer is probably a compromise."

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Overreaches. The author qualifies the approach rather than dismissing it.
  • (B) Contradicted: the landscape "may resemble no particular past at all".
  • (D) Reverses the passage: the approach is "harder to evaluate".

questions.stemHtml: Each of the following is presented as a difficulty with restoring land to its state before human influence EXCEPT:

options.html: In many regions no such state lies within reach of reconstruction.
Changes in climate and soils may prevent the old species from persisting.
Maintaining the restored community may require continual intervention.
Local residents may oppose the return of large grazing animals and predators.

questions.explanationHtml:
Why D is the exception: Opposition from local residents is never mentioned.

The difficulties the passage does give:

  • (A) "No such state within reach of reconstruction".

questions.stemHtml: The passage below is followed by four alternative summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.
bodyHtml: Standardised tests are often criticised for reducing a student's abilities to a single number. The criticism is fair, but it overlooks what the tests replaced. Before them, admission to selective schools frequently depended on interviews and recommendations, which rewarded familiarity with the manners of the class that conducted them. A single number is a crude measure of ability, but it is a measure that a stranger can earn without an introduction.

options.html: Standardised tests measure ability far more accurately than the interviews and recommendations that preceded them.
Crude as they are, standardised tests let outsiders compete on terms earlier methods denied them.
Because interviews favoured the privileged, criticism of standardised tests is unjustified.
Standardised tests should be supplemented by interviews in order to capture abilities that a number misses.

questions.explanationHtml:
Why B is right: It keeps the concession (tests are crude) and the counterpoint (tests are open to outsiders, unlike the interviews they replaced).

Why the others are wrong:

  • (A) Contradicted: a single number is "a crude measure". The paragraph doesn't claim greater accuracy.
  • (C) This is the closest trap. The paragraph says "The criticism is fair". It adds context; it does not reject the criticism.
  • (D) The paragraph makes no recommendation.

questions.explanationHtml:
What the sentence needs: "The problem, it turned out, was not the wait but the boredom of it." "It turned out" reports a discovery, so it must come after the experiment that revealed it.

Gap Verdict
1 Too early. Nothing has yet been tried.
2 Locally plausible, because it follows the engineers' failure. But the discovery would then come before the mirrors that revealed it.
3 The result hasn't been reported yet.
4 Correct. The complaints fell although the wait was unchanged, which leads straight to the conclusion "it turned out".
